O/A Level papers leak likely originated abroad, NA committee told. ISLAMABAD: A parliamentary committee was informed on Monday that the leakage of O/A level papers had originated likely from some other country as no evidence was found to establish its link with Pakistan. The National Assembly Standing Committee on Federal Education and Professional Training, which met with acting Chairman Anjum Aqeel Khan in the chair, besides other agenda items discussed the papers leakage issue of O/A level exams. The committee was informed that the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA), after examining the matter, “found no evidence to establish that the leakage had originated from Pakistan.” The committee was further informed that NCCIA does not have direct access to servers located abroad, which limits its ability to independently trace the source, location and mechanism of any alleged leakage occurring through overseas servers. Lawmakers express concern over growing menace of narcotics in educational institutions In May this year, the government had ordered a probe into the alleged leakage of Cambridge examination papers, directing NCCIA to investigate in coordination with Cambridge Assessment International Education (CAIE) amid concerns raised by parents and students over the alleged leakage of some papers. Meanwhile, the committee expressed grave concern over the growing menace of narcotics in educational institutions and observed that the increasing reports of drug use and supply to students required immediate, coordinated and result-oriented action by the concerned authorities. The committee stressed the need for an effective coordination mechanism among the Anti-Narcotics Force (ANF), police, Higher Education Commission (HEC) and Federal Directorate of Education (FDE) to identify the sources of drug supply and prevent the involvement of criminal elements in and around educational institutions. The committee said the responsibility for ensuring a safe, secure and drug-free learning environment requires a coordinated response involving educational institutions, law-enforcement agencies and regulatory authorities with clear responsibilities, effective monitoring and strict enforcement. The committee sought verified data on reported cases of drug use and supply in educational institutions, including the number and nature of cases, action taken by the concerned authorities, the mechanism adopted for inter-agency coordination and details of the penalties and punishments awarded to those found involved. The committee observed that mere establishment of committees and formulation of policies would not be sufficient unless accompanied by effective implementation, regular monitoring and visible action against those responsible for supplying narcotics to students. The meeting was informed that Anti-Drug and Tobacco Committees had been established in higher educational institutions to monitor and address issues relating to drug and tobacco use among students. The members, however, stressed that such institutional mechanisms must be strengthened and linked with law-enforcement and regulatory authorities to ensure timely reporting, investigation and action in cases involving narcotics. Meanwhile, the committee stressed the need to make the programmes of National Vocational and Technical Training Commission (NAVTTC) more outcome-oriented and aligned with international labour market requirements. The meeting observed that the global employment landscape was changing rapidly, particularly in the Middle East, and emphasised the importance of continuously assessing emerging demand for skilled manpower in international markets. Similarly, Federal Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (FBISE) informed the meeting that pursuant to the recommendations of the subcommittee, a number of measures had been introduced to facilitate students with dyslexia during examinations. These measures included provision of additional time and assistance in reading the question paper to students requiring such support. The committee stressed the need for regular psychological support and the availability of trained remedial teachers in educational institutions to identify learning difficulties at an early stage and provide appropriate assistance to affected students in the classroom. A member stated that legislation relating to dyslexia had also been enacted by the Punjab Assembly, highlighting the need for a comprehensive and uniform approach to address the educational needs of children with dyslexia. The Inter Boards Coordination Commission (IBCC) informed the committee that it would take up the matter with all boards to promote uniform measures and ensure that appropriate facilities and support mechanisms for students with dyslexia were adopted nationwide. New US rules change how international students can stay in America. WASHINGTON: A major change in the US immigration system is set to take effect on Tuesday, requiring international students to keep closer track of how long they are authorised to remain in the country. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is ending the longstanding “duration of status” system for F-1 students and replacing it with a fixed period of admission. Under the new rule, F-1 students will generally be admitted for the length of the academic programme listed on their Form I-20, up to four years, with a 30-day period to arrive before the programme begins and 30 days to prepare for departure after the programme or authorised post-completion training ends. Students who need additional time to complete their current programme, begin a new programme, or undertake post-completion OPT or STEM OPT will have to take additional steps. They may apply to US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) for an extension of stay, or leave the United States and seek a new period of admission from Customs and Border Protection when they return. DHS advises students to work with their college’s designated school official before applying for an extension. Students seeking an extension must file Form I-539 with USCIS after receiving the appropriate recommendation on an updated Form I-20. What happens to students already in America? The change does not mean that every F-1 student currently in the United States has to file a new application on Tuesday. Students who are in the United States in F-1 status under the existing duration of status system on September 15 may remain without applying for an extension until the applicable programme or OPT/STEM OPT end date, subject to the transition rules. For these students, the transition period generally runs no later than November 14, 2030. There is an important exception involving travel. Current F-1 students who leave the United States after Sept 15 may be readmitted under the new fixed-period system, rather than continuing under duration of status system. Students who are considering international travel should therefore speak with their designated school official before leaving the country. New rules for students’ academic plans The rule also imposes new restrictions on changes during an F-1 student’s academic career. Among other changes, undergraduate students generally cannot change their educational level or major during the first year of a program without an exception for extenuating circumstances. Graduate-level students face additional restrictions on changing educational levels, majors and transferring schools. The rule also reduces the departure period after completion of a program or post-completion OPT/STEM OPT from the previous 60 days to 30 days for students subject to the new system. New immigration forms The Sept 15 change also affects USCIS paperwork. Students filing Form I-539, used to request an extension or change of nonimmigrant status, or Form I-765, used to apply for employment authorisation, should use the new editions required by USCIS beginning Tuesday. Students should check the edition date before filing because USCIS will not provide a grace period for use of the previous editions. For international students, the most important point is that Sept. 15 is not a blanket deadline to leave America or file a new application. It marks the beginning of a new system in which admission is tied to a specific period, and students who need additional time may have to obtain an extension or a new period of admission. Universities urge students to check travel, immigration records Major US universities are advising international students to pay particular attention to travel plans and their Form I-94 as the new rules take effect. Harvard University, Yale University, Columbia University, Cornell University and Stanford University have issued guidance explaining the changes and urging students to consult their international offices before making immigration or travel decisions. Yale says students already in the United States under the old “duration of status” system generally do not need to take immediate action on Sept 15. But students who travel abroad and return after that date will generally receive a new I-94 with a specific “admit until” date. Yale advises students to check the I-94 after every international trip. Harvard similarly warns that international travel after Sept 15 can affect future OPT and extension-of-stay planning. Its international office advises students to understand the consequences before making travel plans. Columbia and Cornell have also published detailed guidance on the transition rules, while Stanford has warned that F-1 and J-1 students will no longer be admitted under the D/S notation after the rule takes effect. The message from the universities is essentially the same: students should not assume that Sept 15 itself requires them to leave or file a new application, but they should understand their individual I-94, program end date, OPT plans and the consequences of international travel. The Department of Homeland Security is also ending the “duration of status” system for J-1 exchange visitors and certain I-visa holders, including representatives of foreign information media. They too will generally be admitted for a fixed period rather than indefinitely for the duration of their program or assignment. J-1 participants who need additional time will generally have to seek an extension of stay, while the rules for I representatives are tied to the length of their media assignment. The change does not apply broadly to other major nonimmigrant categories such as H-1B, L-1, O-1 or B-1/B-2 visas, which already operate under fixed periods of admission.

Rethinking relief. THE prime minister’s decision to subsidise petrol purchases for motorcycle and small-car owners is understandable amid consumer outcry against high fuel rates. But it is unlikely to offer much relief. The Rs75bn package may sound substantial but is barely a fraction of annual petrol sales. Its reach will be narrower because eligibility depends on conditions such as vehicle and SIM ownership . A monthly subsidy of Rs2,000 for motorcycles and Rs3,000 for small cars may help households, but cannot shield them from sustained global oil price increases. Nor does it assist those who rely on public transport. The question that arises is whether the government is trying to soften the political impact of another fuel price shock. The government must rethink the relief architecture. The BISP National Socio-Economic Registry already has a mechanism to target assistance by household income. Additional support through this system would be more equitable than subsidising a particular fuel purchase. Cash transfers are preferable because recipients can decide whether they need petrol, bus fare, food or another essential. Fuel subsidies make that choice for them and risk encouraging consumption of an imported commodity when foreign exchange pressures are rising. The demand is for a cut in the petroleum levy for broader relief. But the government has little fiscal space for that. Slashing it would create another fiscal hole. Islamabad should, instead, work with the provinces to support public transport users through targeted — and transparent — assistance. The other problem that subsidies cannot solve concerns rising prices of food and other essentials . Fuel price hikes are passed on by transporters and traders to consumers through higher fares and commodity prices; reductions rarely produce equivalent decreases. Provincial and district administrations must monitor this asymmetric pricing more seriously. The global oil market outlook offers little comfort due to the uncertainty caused by the Middle East conflict. Petrol was around $135 a barrel at the end of last week, against the $120-122 benchmark underlying domestic calculations. Every $1 increase in the global benchmark is estimated to add around Rs1.80 per litre to domestic petrol prices. A sustained $10 rise in annual average oil prices could add $1bn-$1.25bn to Pakistan’s import bill, further draining scarce foreign exchange. The pressure could intensify in winter as lower hydropower generation increases reliance on imported fuels and raises electricity costs. The government’s dilemma is clear: higher fuel prices fuel inflation and hurt households, while subsidies put pressure on imports and the fiscal deficit. It has no painless option. Relief must therefore follow need, not vehicle ownership. A poor household using public transport deserves no less consideration than a relatively better-off motorcycle or a small car owner. Burdens of politicians. IT was a humid Sunday afternoon in Islamabad. The small pharmacy was empty with just one man behind the cash counter. A woman approached him, prescription and medicines in hand. She was simply but not shabbily dressed. But she still returned a quarter of the medication once the bill was generated. The man behind the counter explained the bill was around Rs4,000, and she returned about Rs1,000 worth of medication. This took place at a pharmacy in the heart of Islamabad, where real estate sells or rents at eye-watering prices. There was no doctor nearby or a hospital. The woman, chances are, lived close by. It is not a dramatic story or one that really shocks. Tell it to a group of people and they will nod, and, in fact, recount similar stories. Of people’s difficulties. The loans they have taken. How someone got a utility bill higher than their salary. How a colleague had switched from his car to a motorbike. How another had begun shopping for lower-quality food. Conversations such as these abound. And this is before the past week when petrol hikes — even those of a daily kind — had begun to hit the headlines. People are now taking bets on when the price of petrol will hit 400 — a far more probable prospect than the cricket team managing a respectable score. That the government realises the impact of the petrol hikes is evident from its announcement to relaunch its subsidy scheme . There is little clarity on how effective the last one had been and how long it lasted, but it’s now back with some tweaks. Ask the government to reduce the petrol levy, and suddenly the big bad IMF enters the conversation; the same IMF which can’t get the government to impose a proper tax on traders or agriculture income or even stop it from giving relief to real estate. Apparently, the petrol levy is the red line. There is little conversation about what inflationary impact this petrol hike will have. And of course, there is little conversation about what inflationary impact this petrol hike will have on food, transport and more — what will happen to the electricity bills, and what this new cycle of inflation will do to already weakened purchasing power. Before the reader rolls her eyes at my audacity to write a piece on the economy, let me clarify that I am about to do no such thing. This is simply going to be a clutch-my-pearls piece on the callousness of the ruling elite. It doesn’t get simpler than that. Long before the Iran war and its impact on the global economy, Pakistan’s human story was already a matter of shame. Our infant mortality rate (46 to 58 deaths per 1,000 births) is higher than the rest of the region and comparable to Afghanistan and Yemen. Nearly 20 per cent of the population has an insufficient caloric intake, and around 40pc of children under five years are malnourished and suffer from stunting — in this, Pakistan is comparable to countries hit by conflict and civil war. The numbers are not recent so as to be linked to the economic mess of the past few years. This is the real story, with facts and figures, along with our own experiences and the anecdotes we all hear of the suffering of the people. But for those ruling us, there is little empathy or awareness of the crisis. This may seem a bit harsh but what else does one say when governments are incapable of curbing even their own lavish personal lifestyles in the face of human misery? The prime minister and his deputy, it seems, spend more time abroad than in the country. Newly born babies recently died in a hospital fire in the heart of the capital, petrol is going up faster than pollution, and we already know he is off to New York on the 20th to tell the world about Pakistan’s efforts in mediation. When one’s home is on fire, shouldn’t saving it be more important? A rhetorical question — for soon we will be subjected to a bunch of ministers and advisers walking on the tarmac and entering a plane. The rest are not far behind. Just recently both the president and the chief minister of Punjab travelled to Europe on personal visits on private planes. And only widespread criticism forced them both to make public the information that the trips were paid for personally. As if anyone needed any more proof of such disconnect from the lives of ordinary Pakistanis. The president was on a personal visit while the party and the government he heads was announcing war on proposals to divide Sindh . If the situation was that dire politically, shouldn’t he have been in Pakistan and in the province? And the Punjab CM — two-and-a-half years later — does not seem to realise that a display of wealth in these times is just poor judgement. Despite the widespread criticism of the aircraft purchased by the Punjab government, it was used for a personal trip. However, this criticism is simply water off a duck’s back. The display of a lavish wedding followed all of this. This is not to say that politicians should not be allowed private lives; they have every right to it. However, extensive footage and images displaying the grandeur of an event is simply a poor decision. No one expects Pakistan’s ruling elite to behave like their counterparts in the West where ministers carry their own baggage and fly economy. We are far too realistic to expect miracles here but a little discretion can do no harm. And for once, it is not enough to argue that there are powerful people in Pakistan who perhaps enjoy even more perks than politicians but are not spoken about. Indeed, those who take part in electoral exercise and claim to be popular have different burdens than those who simply wield power. And the people in government need to understand this difference. The writer is a journalist. Published in Dawn, September 15th, 2026

To heal a divided family. CENTURIES before Charles Darwin theorised our shared human evolution from the fish, multiple traditions linked humanity to a single common fold. The 18th BRICS summit in Delhi saw Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi as the host leaning on the Sanskrit phrase ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam’ — the world is a family — to underpin the spirit of unity, which unfortunately eludes much of mankind. The ancient aphorism is a good but an overstretched reminder of seeing everybody as an equal human being. Some would say that there was perhaps a greater need to find a phrase that frames all Indians as one family before stretching it to include the world. A problem with citing one’s ancient aphorisms at international conferences is that it begins to resemble the Sadda Mian complex. Sadda Mian was a roundly admired elderly Afghan member of Bhopal’s royal family. He wou­­ld walk along the promenade abutting Bhopal’s vast lake called Bhadbhada, which, he decided, was the largest water body in the world. Another characteristic unique to Sadda Mian was that he fed his domesticated quails with his mouth, tucking the tiny grains of food behind the lower lip. The late thespian Dilip Kumar told me about his invitation to Sadda Mian to visit Bombay where the actor took the genial Pathan to watch the Arabian Sea from the city’s Marine Drive. Sadda Mian, his sherwani unbuttoned and fluttering in the breeze, was so awestruck by the sea’s expanse that he exclai­med gently: “Kya haqeeqat hai Bhadbhade ki!” Sadda Mian’s dumbfounded response translates as: ‘Where does any Bhadbhada hold a chance!’ I looked up a few random traditions from across the lands and seas that don’t seem too different in the spirit of acknowledging the world as a family. But few among them, if any, would be found jumping ecstatically as Newton did watching an apple fall from a tree. There was a time in the early days of Narendra Modi’s rule that the foreign ministry printed and distributed copies of the Bhagavad Gita to foreign dignitaries. In the bargain, the ministry displaced coffee-table books of the Taj, Ajanta caves and Madurai temples. I am not aware of Israel handing out the Torah, or the Vatican presenting the Bible to esteemed visitors, nor does Saudi Arabia or Iran make it a point to offer return gifts of the Holy Quran to visiting dignitaries. Or for that matter, would a privileged guest, returning from China, come home with an officially gifted copy of Mao Zedong Thoughts, or more recently Xi Jinping Thoughts? I bought the Xi book on Amazon. If the world is a family, which it is, talking to the neighbour and sorting out the problem bilaterally is mature. So yes, the world is a family, but what kind of a family? The BRICS summit sought to address some aspects of the troubling question but, by all accounts, it’s going to be a long trudge. Modi said BRICS has come of age — in the sense that the leaders of the UAE and Iran agreeing to meet and not pressing their case too hard to enable a summit statement was an achievement. One could have accepted the condemnation of the terror attack in Pahalgam and reference to cross-border terrorism as a victory for India. But Pakistan had condemned the attack too. Actually, the BRICS summit in Xiamen in 2017 had gone several steps further when under President Xi’s stewardship it named some extremist outfits allegedly based in Pakistan together with Taliban groups and local security elements for censure. If the world is a family, which it is, talking to the neighbour and sorting out the problem bilaterally is mature. The world brotherhood will applaud. And, yes, the word ‘family’ loses its meaning when someone is seen standing with an aggressor like Israel and visits the country on the eve of Israel’s assassination of a revered supreme leader of a far friendlier country. Also, if the world is a family, let’s stop patronising lynch mobs against fellow humans everywhere. It’s not unlikely that the BRICS summit’s statement slamming Israel’s occupation of Lebanon was a sign of the coming of age. Xi Jinping dominated the show. He said BRICS should become a peacemaker. There needs to be peace within the family. Looking objectively at the idea of global brotherhood with all its warts and wrinkles, the Nehruvian ideal of non-alignment was quite representative of the quest. But Xi, too, has made a forceful intervention to make BRICS more proactive in its quest for global brotherhood. And he stated that BRICS must be a “pioneer in upholding peace and stability”, emphasising that the group needs to actively manage global hotspot issues by addressing both their symptoms and root causes. He clearly outlined a four-point plan for West Asia, focusing on peaceful coexistence, respect for national sovereignty, adhering to international law, and regional development. It was Xi who reiterated the necessity of pushing for an immediate ceasefire at all the hotspots in West Asia to establish a lasting two-state solution for Palestine to resolve the nub of the crisis. Unlike the Sanskrit phrase cited by Modi, which seems ornamental and ill-fitting given India’s domestic and foreign entanglements with strife, the ancient South African ideal of Ubuntu very crucially was at play when apartheid was dismantled in the country. Nelson Mandela and Desmond Tutu leaned on the Zulu phrase ‘Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu’. Strikingly similar to the Sanskrit worldview, Ubuntu assured every race and community in the country of equity and equality. The phrase literally means: ‘A person is a person through other persons’ or ‘I am because we are’. The Abrahamic scriptures carry similar messages of a united mankind. The Galatians 3:28 in the Bible says: “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” This isn’t dissimilar to India’s Maha Upanishad defining narrow-mindedness as calculating ‘this person is a relative, that one is a stranger’. A tricky proposition for Modi to grasp. The writer is Dawn’s correspondent in Delhi. jawednaqvi@gmail.com Published in Dawn, September 15th, 2026

How India's transnational repression cases expose unequal accountability across borders. Simonetta Fornasiero Fifteen years before a guilty plea in New York exposed an Indian government employee’s alleged role in a plot to assassinate a Sikh activist, the body of a 15-year-old Bangladeshi girl hung from the India-Bangladesh border fence for hours. Felani Khatun was shot dead by India’s Border Security Force on January 7, 2011, as she crossed the frontier with her father near Kurigram. The image of her body caught in the wire became one of Bangladesh’s most searing symbols of its unequal relationship with its larger neighbour. Yet the years that followed brought neither a final sense of justice for her family nor an end to such killings. The scale extends far beyond the cases that became national symbols. Ain o Salish Kendra data show that the BSF shot and killed 285 Bangladeshi civilians between 2014 and February 2026, an average of nearly 24 a year. A further ten Bangladeshis were killed in BSF-linked border violence during the first half of 2026, according to the rights organisation. That history gives Bangladesh a distinct vantage point from which to view the cases of Hardeep S ingh Nijjar in Canada and Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in the United States . For Ottawa and Washington, these cases opened a relatively new debate over alleged Indian transnational repression. For Bangladeshis, the central issue is older and closer to home. When Indian security interests collide with the lives and rights of people beyond India’s borders, who is powerful enough to demand accountability? The answer, so far, appears to depend heavily on where the victim is found. The reckoning In February 2026, Nikhil Gupta pleaded guilty in a Manhattan federal court to murder-for-hire and related charges in a plot targeting Pannun, a US citizen and prominent advocate of a separate Sikh state. According to the US Justice Department, Gupta acted at the direction of Vikash Yadav, who worked for the Indian government from the Cabinet Secretariat, which houses the Research and Analysis Wing (RAW), India’s main external intelligence agency. Prosecutors said Yadav supplied information about the target and agreed to a $100,000 payment. The supposed hitman was an undercover US law-enforcement officer. The plea does not establish that Prime Minister Narendra Modi or his cabinet authorised the operation. Nor does it prove the outstanding charge against Yadav, who has not been arrested. It does, however, establish Gupta’s criminal participation and give judicial weight to the US allegation that an Indian government employee directed the plot. India has described the episode as the misconduct of an individual acting outside state policy. The Canadian picture is more complicated. Nijjar, a Canadian Sikh activist, was shot dead outside a gurdwara in British Columbia in June 2023. Canada’s then prime minister, Justin Trudeau, later spoke of credible allegations of Indian state involvement , which New Delhi denied. In July 2026, U.S. and Canadian authorities announced charges against Lawrence Bishnoi and members of an alleged transnational criminal network in connection with Nijjar’s murder and other crimes. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said the charges announced at that stage did not produce evidence linking Indian government officials to them. Bangladesh’s own experience with the murder of student leader Sharif Osman Hadi provides a different but instructive comparison. Hadi was shot in Dhaka in December 2025, and Bangladeshi investigators say the principal suspects fled to India, where they were subsequently arrested. There is no public evidence that the Indian state directed Hadi’s killing. The parallel lies instead in what followed: although India and Bangladesh agreed in April 2026 that the suspects would be returned under their extradition treaty, by July Dhaka said it had completed the required legal and diplomatic formalities and was still awaiting India’s approval . The case became another test of how readily accountability can stall when evidence and suspects cross into a more powerful neighbour’s jurisdiction. That was not a judicial exoneration of India. The prosecution of alleged gang members and the wider inquiry into foreign interference are separate questions. Canadian officials had previously alleged that Indian representatives used the Bishnoi network to intimidate or attack Sikh separatists. The defensible conclusion is not that Canada cleared India while the United States condemned it. It is that the public evidence has developed differently in the two jurisdictions, and that the Pannun case has gone further in establishing an operational link to an Indian official. As Meenakshi Ganguly, deputy Asia director at Human Rights Watch, notes, “There are also serious concerns about transnational repression targeting diaspora Indians or foreign nationals, including those of Indian origin, for criticising the Modi administration.” Lack of accountability Bangladesh should resist the temptation to collapse every case into a single conspiracy. BSF shootings at the frontier arise from border enforcement, alleged smuggling and irregular crossings, but that legal distinction must not erase the question of impunity. A suspected border offence is not a death sentence, and every fatal shooting requires an independent investigation capable of producing accountability. The figures show why this is not merely a historical grievance. Ain o Salish Kendra recorded 34 Bangladeshis killed in BSF firing or torture in 2025 — 24 in shootings and 10 allegedly following physical torture, while further deaths were reported in 2026, including two Bangladeshis killed along the Kasba border in May. In September 2024, Bangladeshi schoolgirl Swarna Das was shot near the Moulvibazar border. Like Felani, her age and the circumstances of her death transformed an otherwise routine diplomatic protest into a national symbol. Yet repeated pledges by Indian and Bangladeshi border commanders to reduce killings to zero have not produced zero deaths. “The BSF does not operate beyond borders. But it has used excessive force to attack unarmed people, mostly Bangladeshi irregular migrants, and in some cases cattle rustlers or smugglers,” Ganguly says. “In our investigations, we have found that the troops used disproportionate force, and that the authorities failed to hold people to account for these violations.” Lethal measures That deterrent logic took an especially troubling form in March 2026. An internal BSF memo reportedly asked field units to assess the feasibility of using venomous snakes and crocodiles in riverine stretches where fencing is difficult, saying the proposal was “in line with Home Minister Amit Shah’s directions”. The idea had not been implemented, and former BSF director general Prakash Singh called it “silly”, warning that reptiles could not distinguish between Bangladeshis and Indians living near the border. Even as a proposal, however, it illustrates the human rights danger of treating irregular migration as a threat to be repelled through potentially lethal means rather than a matter for arrest, verification and due process. The Indian record shows that the accountability problem is not confined to one frontier. In Manipur, petitioners asked India’s Supreme Court to investigate 1,528 alleged extrajudicial executions committed over several decades; the court held that even security forces operating under special powers could not claim immunity for excessive or retaliatory force. In Kashmir’s 2010 Machil case , soldiers were convicted by a military court of killing three civilians and presenting them as militants, although later legal developments showed how fragile such accountability could be. These cases do not prove responsibility for Nijjar, Pannun or any specific Bangladeshi death. They reveal a long institutional struggle over lethal force and effective scrutiny of security personnel. “It is the Indian government’s lack of political will to end, or at least reduce, the number of killings at the border,” says Ali Riaz, distinguished professor of political science at Illinois State University. “It also sends a message about the unequal relationship and demonstrates a perception within the Indian establishment that Bangladeshi lives matter less.” Power asymmetry The contrast with the United States is stark. Washington had the jurisdiction, investigative reach and political leverage to run an undercover operation, extradite Gupta, put evidence before a federal court and secure a guilty plea. Bangladesh has no comparable leverage over Indian personnel. Its tools are diplomatic protests, border-force meetings and demands for Indian investigations — mechanisms that depend heavily on the cooperation of the same state whose agents are accused. The unresolved effort to extradite Sheikh Hasina sharpens the same point. India and Bangladesh signed an extradition treaty in 2013 and amended it in 2016 to facilitate the transfer of fugitives. Dhaka has repeatedly sought Hasina’s return from India and renewed its formal request in April 2026 after she was convicted and sentenced to death in absentia over the 2024 crackdown. India has said it is examining the request under its legal procedures, while Bangladesh said in August that it was still awaiting a response. The treaty permits refusal where an offence is considered political or an accusation is not made in good faith, so delay alone does not establish a treaty violation. It does, however, demonstrate how political judgment can determine whether a formal legal framework produces accountability in practice. That asymmetry was especially visible during Sheikh Hasina’s rule , when exceptionally close strategic ties with New Delhi often encouraged Dhaka to manage border deaths as irritants within a valuable relationship rather than as a sustained accountability crisis. The political rupture after Hasina’s fall has sharpened public criticism of India, but anger alone will not protect border communities. “Unfortunately, Bangladesh has little leverage in this regard,” Riaz says. “But power asymmetry should not determine the relationship between two neighbours; it should be based on mutual respect and dignity.” Riaz argues that India’s conduct violates international law and norms, and that responsibility does not rest with Dhaka alone. “It is also incumbent on members of Indian civil society and human rights organisations to speak up and hold their government accountable, as it is on the international community,” he points out. The cost of unequal relationship Bangladesh needs a consistent policy built around transparent casualty data, prompt joint investigations, published findings, compensation for families and an agreed protocol restricting firearms to situations involving an imminent threat to life. Dhaka should press for measurable bilateral commitments and invite independent rights scrutiny. The Nijjar and Pannun cases may not resolve every allegation against India, but they do reveal what accountability looks like when the affected state has the power to insist on it. A US court could convert intelligence into admissible evidence and a criminal conviction. On the Bangladesh border, families have too often received a body, a protest note and another promise of restraint. Felani’s image endures because it captures the human cost of an unequal relationship in which security claims repeatedly outran legal accountability. If the Pannun prosecution has established anything of wider significance, it is that strategic partnership need not require silence when a state official is implicated in lethal wrongdoing. Bangladesh should demand no less for its own citizens.

Ex-Google DeepMind researcher adds to warnings that AI could 'kill all humans'. A former Google DeepMind employee on Monday became the latest AI researcher to warn that the technology could “kill all humans”, saying time could be running out to avoid the outcome. Public alarm about the potential danger posed by AI is growing, after Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon said last week he had resigned, in part because the “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger then responded to Coxon’s comments, saying he was correct and that he believed there was a greater than 10 per cent chance that AI could kill all humans within the next decade. “I recently resigned from Google DeepMind, where I worked on AGI safety and alignment research,” Bilal Chughtai wrote on X. “I earnestly believe that AI has the potential to kill us all, and that we might be running out of time to avoid this outcome.” Chughtai, who co-authored research papers while at Google DeepMind, worked there as a research engineer and left the company in July 2026, according to his LinkedIn profile . Google did not respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours. Following recent concerns, Anthropic Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Dario Amodei called for a slowdown in the pace of advanced AI development over the weekend, winning rare backing from SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and sparking a debate over AI “doomerism”. Chughtai also said that navigating AI safely was possible but would require coordination “to avoid this manic race between AI companies”. “We need to pace AI development to a speed that society can handle, where emerging risks can be addressed before extreme harm is realised,” he added. President Donald Trump, however, has dismissed the warnings , saying on social media the AI industry’s call for regulation is a “hoax.”

These Baloch fishermen don’t want fast food. The people living along Balochistan’s beaches have always fought to defend the sea that feeds them. For years, fishermen from Gwadar to Lasbela accused large trawlers from Sindh of sweeping up everything in their path when they entered Balochistan’s twelve-nautical-mile waters. Their prohibited wire nets or “gujja” trapped juvenile fish, breeding stock and species with scant commercial value, leaving little behind. This fight defined the Haq Do Tehreek movement that united thousands around a single demand: save the sea before it is emptied. Today, that friction has turned inwards over a fish that barely fits in your palm and is banned from fishing: the Beechum (or Paseli). Scientists call it the Fringescale Sardine because it rarely grows beyond 11cm and spends its life moving in dense schools. “We never used to catch it,” says 65-year-old Ghulam Muhammad who spent his life in the waters off Ormara. “The bigger fish follow these schools of Beechum and those are the ones we actually wanted,” he says. “If we wipe out Beechum, one day we will lose the larger fish too.“ This understanding shaped the trade along the Makran coast long before governments spoke of marine conservation. “Earn your livelihood from the sea but don’t set fire to the fishermen’s fields,” as Gwadar activist Javed Hayat puts it. Time and money High-powered speedboats, known locally as “kayak” changed the game so the younger lot don’t want to spend days searching for tuna and king mackerel. A fishing trip used to demand patience because the Yak-dar or heavy wooden boats were slow, but could remain at sea for days, carrying enough food, water and fuel. Crews waited for the fish they wanted rather than chasing whatever could be sold quickest. Unlike the old wooden boats that took nearly a day to reach distant fishing grounds, these speedboats can make the same journey in less than three hours so a crew can now return the same day and head back out again the next morning. Their numbers have rapidly grown, say local activists, because the cross-border diesel trade with Iran has made it possible for rich newcomers to enter the fishing business. Your browser does not support the video tag. As catch declined, fishermen grew impoverished. Today many of them don’t even own their nets but have to borrow gear, fuel and equipment from seafood processors or factory owners under agreements that require them to sell their catch back to them. Now that market forces control the decision-making, these businesses are happy to pay for a fish that was once left in the sea. Demand from China and Malaysia for the sardines has gone up and the men are just following the market, explains Nagman Baloch, the general secretary of the Seafood Association. So now, from Sindh to Sonmiani the waters have been depleted by persistently hoovering up one of the last links in the food chain. Balochistan’s coastline stretches more than 730 kilometres, and fisheries support the livelihoods of over seventy percent of the province’s coastal population. Yet official assessments conclude that almost all conventional marine resources within the province’s jurisdiction are now either fully exploited or overexploited. Some of the most valuable commercial species, including snappers, groupers, croakers and shrimp have declined to critical levels. The intensive harvesting of juvenile fish and small pelagic species is preventing stocks from recovering. Law and order Pressure is being exerted on the government and Fisheries Department by both sides for and against the ban. It would be counterintuitive to lift it as that would destroy the very ecosystem the fishermen once fought to protect. But times are tight and many men argue they just can’t afford to leave Beechum in the sea. Some of the resentment and anger comes from the unequal application of the ban. “If it is banned, then ban it across the entire Balochistan coast,” says Younis Anwar of the Gwadar Fishermen’s Alliance (Gwadar Mahigeer Ittehad). “Why should it only be enforced in Gwadar tehsil?” No one is against ecological conservation but that is a conversation that applies to everyone. “If the whole coast is covered by the ban, we will support it,” he says. “But everyone should be treated the same.” That said, policing the waters is, to him, a waste of time. The government would do better to create artificial reefs as breeding grounds and push for the use of marine-friendly nets. “If the fish increase,” he says, “people won’t have to depend on Beechum.” Slip right through The growing dependence on catching the small fish has made the men fight over even the size of the mesh in a net. Government officials explain it in inches. Fishermen explain it in “chamag”. Younis Anwar stretches out his arm. From the tip of his middle finger to his elbow, he traces an imaginary line. “This is how we measure our nets,” he says. If sixteen mesh openings fit between those two points, they call it a “16-chammag” net. It is 2.5 inches of mesh officially. “This lets the small fish escape,” Younis explains. “Only the fish that have grown large enough remain in the net.” As catch declined the demand for small fish increased, and the mesh kept shrinking. Sardines and prawns need a 28-chammag which won’t let anything slip through. The fisheries law prescribes minimum mesh size that broadly corresponds to the 16-chammag net. Ahmed Nadeem of the Fisheries Department says they eventually stepped in after objections over the widespread use of Number 28 nets. Following a series of meetings at the Deputy Commissioner’s office involving fishermen, local officials and the Fisheries Department, the authorities prohibited the 28-chammag nets. The negotiations ended with a compromise, fishermen agreed to replace them with 25-chammag nets. But even the 25-chammags are still finer than what the law technically permits. Activist K. B. Firaq sees the Beechum debate as the latest chapter in a long-running story. Several species had thinned out long before fishermen began arguing over sardines. His surest proof is that younger fishermen no longer recognize their names. Most fishermen, he says, are no longer deciding what they want to catch. They are catching what the market is willing to buy. The tragedy, in his view, is that everyone earns something today while the sea absorbs the cost. Constitution must remain supreme, every exercise of public authority must be within its limits: FCC CJ. Federal Constitutional Court (FCC) Chief Justice Aminuddin Khan on Tuesday stressed constitutional supremacy and observed that every public exercise must be in accordance with it. “The Constitution must remain supreme, and every exercise of the public authority must remain within its constitutional boundaries,” he said while addressing an event in Islamabad. The FCC chief justice noted that the Constitution was the “supreme expression of the collective will of the people”. He went on to say that every institution created under it derived its authority from it and remained subject to its limits. “Therefore, the fundamental philosophy that must guide the court is simple yet profound.” The FCC was created as part of the judicial restructuring done under the 27th Constitutional Amendment, passed in November 2025. The contentious amendment, passed by Parliament amid the opposition’s outcry, had been criticised by some legal experts as a means of dethroning the Supreme Court (SC) as the country’s highest judicial forum, ceding that position to the FCC. Justice Aminuddin described the creation of the FCC as an “important institutional development in the constitutional history of Pakistan”. He highlighted that constitutional adjudication occupied a “unique position in the administration of justice”. “It concerns not merely disputes between individuals but questions touching the very structure of the state, the distribution of constitutional powers, the protection of fundamental rights and the preservation of the constitutional order.” Recalling the challenges faced by the FCC upon its creation, Justice Aminuddin recalled that the court did not inherit a “fully developed institutional infrastructure” when it was created. “We had to build an institution while simultaneously performing the judicial responsibilities entrusted to us by the Constitution,” he highlighted. “In many respects, we began our journey from scratch,” the top FCC judge remarked. “There was no prolonged period of institutional preparation before justice would begin; the court was established, the judges took their oath, and the constitutional responsibility of adjudication commenced,” he said. Recalling that three benches of the FCC commenced their work on the day the judges took their oath, Justice Aminuddin said that “moment remains a powerful reminder of the spirit with which this institution was born”. He noted that the FCC initially began its functioning from the building of the Islamabad High Court (IHC), before it later moved to its current premises, formerly the Federal Shariat Court’s (FSC) building . In November last year, the government had decided to set up offices for FCC judges within the IHC despite space constraints, as FSC judges had reportedly refused to vacate their building for the newly established constitutional court. “The transition itself was a formidable institutional exercise,” Justice Aminuddin said, adding that the court’s building was constructed about 46 years ago and was originally designed to accommodate around 100 employees. “Today, however, nearly 400 officers, officials and attached staff of this court are working within these premises,” the judge observed. “Space is limited. Facilities are under considerable pressure,” he regretted, pointing out that some officials work in improvised cabins and compact work stations. Justice Aminuddin remarked: “Yet, despite these physical limitations, the work has continued, and it has continued because institutions are ultimately not built by concrete and bricks alone. “Institutions are built by people. They are built by commitments.”

Data centres in Australia: your questions answered. From almost 350 questions, nine experts answer the most common ones you asked.

We may be able to turn off the algorithm, but we can’t escape the misogyny of the manosphere. Important as it is, no amount of social media regulation will meaningfully address the manosphere unless we also dismantle the misogyny that underpins it.
Australia must double down to meet our climate targets. Our new study shows how. Global warming is set to surpass the 1.5°C limit if governments worldwide fail to act.
Too many students have ‘reading anxiety’. New research suggests it is triggered by problems in primary school. Reading anxiety involves excessive worries and apprehensions about reading activities.

What are statins? And can healthy people use them to prevent heart disease and dementia?. New evidence shows more people might benefit from this cholesterol-lowering medication than we previously thought. But that doesn’t mean everyone should take one.

A brief history of collage from 12th century Japan to Sydney today – and your own kitchen table. Collage can be traced back to the invention of paper. Australian artists are still exploring its possibilities today. Here’s how you can, too.

Alice Duncan-Kemp was an empathetic observer of Mithaka culture, but her legacy is complicated. Alice Duncan-Kemp’s books drew on a pastoral childhood in intimate contact with Mithaka people. They formed part of the basis for a 2015 native title determination.
Your say: week beginning September 14. On tobacco tax and sharing the cost of housing: an edited selection of your views.
Data from more than 600 people shows resting heart rates have their own secret rhythm. The rhythms aren’t necessarily tied to hormones, nor any other single cause.

Imported phosphate for fertiliser is expensive – could this homegrown alternative be a solution?. Research shows a phosphorus-rich compound found in wastewater raises uptake by plants and reduces discharge to waterways.

Democrats’ chances of gaining control of Congress at US midterms depend on Iran war. Recent polling shows if the disruption caused by the Trump administration’s war with Iran continues, Democrats will likely gain control of Congress.

Shocks, alchemy and John Howard’s ‘long shadow’ have shaped 21st century Australian politics. New books by George Megalogenis and Paul Strangio consider 21st century Australia: a time of rapid social change with many politicians stuck ‘in a white-bloke past’.

View from The Hill: One Nation would have more people leaving than entering Australia over three years. One Nation has released a radical policy that would see Australia reduce its temporary migrant population by 750,000.

Why strengthening ties with the Global South was a top priority for Putin’s recent diplomacy blitz. The Ukraine war certainly featured in conversations. Tellingly, however, Putin steered many talks with leaders towards fuel, trade and transit.
Why big tech will hate the Australian tax office’s latest ruling. Australia’s laws don’t deal with all the ways local profits are shifted offshore. The ATO aims to close that gap.

Big AI wants to slow down AI research. Is it a safety pause or a strategic retreat?. AI companies are calling for a coordinated pause to progress – but making it work, and keeping AI safe, won’t be easy.

Rinse: Amrita Hepi’s show about beginnings is a mid-career masterpiece. The internationally acclaimed fusion of choreography and monologue, co-created by Hepi with Mish Grigor, is a witty exploration of beginnings.
Trailblazing lawyer Mary Gaudron, a woman of many firsts, leaves a huge and lasting legacy. The first woman judge on the High Court shaped Australian legal history and was an inspiration to many.

All-round condemnation for Pauline Hanson over Indigenous slur. Pauline Hanson’s derogatory remarks about Indigenous people on a podcast last year have been slammed by members of the government, the Liberals and the Nationals.

Five years into AUKUS, what do we have to show for it? We’ve measured progress on three key metrics. Though reliably measuring progress is difficult, it would be disingenuous to say Australia has nothing to show for its investments to date.

Unsustainable – or manageable? We don’t yet know how data centres will impact Australia’s environment. The data centre boom will mean more energy and water use. The real question is how the energy is produced – and where the water comes from.

Australia’s digital duty of care bill needs these three changes to tackle online child sexual exploitation. Tech platforms need to be responsible for reporting online child sexual exploitation rather than relying on victims to do so.

Make ‘em laugh: how One Nation uses comedy to normalise harmful ideas. The party’s Please Explain cartoon series has ignited a political firestorm, but behind the punchlines and backlash is an insidious way to spread propaganda.
Australia’s female economists have been making history for nearly 150 years. It’s time we knew their stories. In a stubbornly male dominated field, how brilliant did a woman have to be to succeed?

It’s been one year since Australia assessed its national climate risk. But have we listened?. Over the past 12 months, the federal government has approved multiple fossil fuel projects and cut climate science funding.

1 in 3 uni students experience serious financial hardship. Could concession cards for all help?. The peak body for Australian universities says the measure would ease cost-of-living pressures for students.

Skipping showers is the latest trend. But is there any science to ‘pheromone’ maxxing?. Animals use pheromones as chemical messengers to attract a mate or mark territory. But human sweat is very different.

Poetry is popular with young Australians, from pop-up readings to poetry slams. Young poets are performing at poetry slams, pop-up events and salons around Australia – and publishing, too. Who are they – and why is poetry so popular?

‘Buy now, pay later’ doesn’t feel like debt. For young people, that can be a big problem. A survey of young New Zealanders finds four in ten didn’t view buy now, pay later as debt. That perception can influence how they use it.

The case for NZ joining the UK in sanctioning Israel over illegal West Bank settlements. The government insists sanctioning Israel is too complex so close to an election. But New Zealand also has obligations under international law it shouldn’t ignore.

Coalition retains clear lead in Victorian Resolve poll, while federal polls are mixed. Labor is likely to lose the Victorian election, but it’s unclear whether the Coalition will be able to govern in majority or need support from One Nation.

Our new research shows humans have maligned bandicoots for decades, making them more vulnerable to extinction. Humans have had a complex relationship with this marsupial, known for its pointy snout, thin tail and large hind feet.

How does unthinkable policy become inevitable? The ‘Overton window’ is one possible answer. It was once deemed crazy to get rid of protective tariffs. Privatising state banks was inconceivable. Both are now commonplace, but how does this happen?

Why Sydney Sweeney’s controversial advert goes beyond sexualising women’s sport. The discussion surrounding the American actor’s ad raises bigger questions about the attention placed on women’s bodies, not just in sport.

Bluster and betrayal: Paul Barry probes how steel tycoon Sanjeev Gupta hoodwinked the powerful. Amid news that 500 jobs will go at the Whyalla steelworks, once owned by Gupta’s GFG Alliance, The Big Steal is a powerful – and timely – work of journalism.

Was there really a female king in ancient Egypt 5,000 years ago? New study says yes. Meretneith was buried in a tomb fit for a male ruler. But for decades, debate has raged over her true royal status.

Poorly fitting sports bras are forcing some women and girls away from sport – new research. Most decision-makers in sport think girls and women would benefit from learning about sports bra design, fit and support. Less than 1% offer this education.

David Hockney: Portraits in Print reveals lesser-known aspects of the celebrated artist. The National Gallery of Australia exhibition showcases the late British artist’s mastery of intimate detail and talent for connection
Hanson ‘regrets’ hurt caused by remark about ‘primitive’ First Nations people. After facing a barrage of criticism for her comments, the One Nation leader says it was not her intention to cause hurt.

175 years of university architecture reflects Australian history. We shouldn’t let that history be lost. University campuses reflect the layers of architectural and landscape styles that have shaped our cities and suburbs.

On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 09/11/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 11 September 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky E-post Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Spara Utskrift 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. He also urged the GSF, which remains far short of its planned 5,500-person strength, to deploy in full without delay. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. Such coordinated attacks are routine, says Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler, but the scale of this campaign was unusual. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. The trip came three days after U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. Trump also said he is willing to meet with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, as he did during his first term. These two unilateral announcements in turn prompted South Korean President Lee Jae-myung to reiterate his call for Seoul to bolster its own defences, for instance by acquiring nuclear-powered submarines and regaining independent control of its military in the event of hostilities. (Its forces would now be under U.S. command in a wartime contingency.) Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. It may now seek to present itself as the main mediator on the Korean peninsula, given its links with Pyongyang. ISRAEL - SYRIA Israeli warplanes bombed the Abu al-Duhur air base in northern Syria early Tuesday morning, in what Israel said was a warning against “deployment” of Turkish military personnel at the site. No casualties were reported. In remarks protesting the strike, Syrian Foreign Minister Assad al-Shaibani said Turkish officers had visited the base three days previously, but only for “training” purposes as Syrian forces refurbish the base. Tom Barrack, the U.S. ambassador to Türkiye who doubles as envoy for Syria, described Israel’s action as “unnecessary”. The backdrop, says Crisis Group expert Noah Bonsey, is an impasse in Israeli-Syrian talks about a bilateral security agreement. In these U.S.-mediated negotiations, under way since last summer, the Syrian government is seeking Israel’s withdrawal from parts of southern Syria it has occupied since December 2024, while Israel presses for limits on Turkish support for the Syrian military, among other security guarantees. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pledged to retain a “buffer zone” in Syria as he campaigns for re-election in October. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Lafta-Gareen fled to the Kenyan capital Nairobi, but his followers have been seeking to reinstate him, making regular incursions into Baidoa from a base on its northern outskirts. They reject the new state president who took office after a hastily organised vote following Lafta-Gareen’s ouster. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says Monday’s attack was the largest and deadliest to date. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. The strikes came as both U.S. President Donald Trump and Iran claimed to have “total control” over the Strait of Hormuz. The Islamic Republic and Oman are in negotiations over a deal to partially reopen this crucial waterway. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says these consultations are part of a scramble by mediators to nudge the U.S. and Iran back into a truce, without which any bilateral understanding about the strait is unlikely to get much traction. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. Just two weeks earlier, clashes broke out between the Ethiopian military and opposing Tigray forces along a different part of the Sudan-Ethiopia border. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. It is another incident revealing the current Israeli government’s agenda for the West Bank, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. The Trump administration, which has sanctioned the ICC for its investigation of Israeli actions in Gaza, called on more African nations to “reclaim their sovereignty” by following in Chad’s footsteps. Crisis Group expert Enrica Picco says some Chadians will welcome N’djamena’s move on these grounds. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Tensions between the TPLF and Addis Ababa have been rising for months, especially after it ousted an interim regional administration established under a 2022 peace deal and reinstalled its own chair as regional president in April. The two sides now accuse each other of soliciting help from one of the main belligerents in Sudan. Independent details of the clashes are scarce, says Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell, but clearly neither side wanted to escalate further at this time. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. Six assailants in the bed of a pickup truck fired assault rifles and threw pipe bombs, stealing the rangers’ weapons and body armour before fleeing. They also wounded six civilians, including three children, one seriously. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Let those who provide shelter and the countries that harbour them know this”. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. U.S. - IRAN The U.S. and Iran continued to trade blows this week, putting Washington’s Middle Eastern allies in the crosshairs of Iranian drone and missile launch teams while U.S. forces enforced a renewed naval blockade of Iran and conducted daily strikes on sites inside the country. On Wednesday, President Donald Trump pledged to “destroy one bridge or power plant” every time Tehran fires at a vessel transiting the Strait of Hormuz – a threat quickly met by warnings of retaliation in kind by the Islamic Republic. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says both sides appear convinced that inflicting greater physical damage and economic pain plays to their strengths, even at the risk of significant escalation. For now, this dynamic is persisting despite efforts by mediators to dial down tensions. YEMEN The Houthi rebels declared a “maritime embargo” on Saudi Arabia Monday, vowing to strike any Saudi-linked vessel passing from the Red Sea through Bab al-Mandab, the strait connecting those waters to the Gulf of Oman. A de facto truce had held between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognised government from 2022 until last week, when Saudi warplanes bombed the Sanaa airport and the Houthis fired missiles at the kingdom in respo nse. On Wednesday, Saudi officials said an oil tanker caught fire after the Houthis struck it near the kingdom’s Red Sea port of Jizan. The foreign ministry in Riyadh said Saudi Arabia would take all necessary measures to defend itself, while U.S. President Donald Trump said the U.S. would inflict “major military punishment” upon both the Houthis and their ally Iran if they attack shipping again. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says the risk of open hostilities, both in the Red Sea and along front lines in Yemen, is rising dramatically. 17 July 2026 CUBA Cuba’s power grid collapsed Tuesday for the third time in less than ten days and the sixth time so far in 2026. The island’s severe energy shortages began in January when the U.S. imposed an oil blockade, triggering a humanitarian crisis. The blockade is part of the Trump administration’s pressure campaign to bring about wholesale political and economic change in Cuba, as negotiations between the two countries stall. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the U.S. appears to be using civilian pain as a weapon in its effort to oust Cuba’s communist regime. Havana should pursue meaningful and much needed reforms, regardless of what the U.S. does. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says that both sides remain nominally open to diplomacy. Stability during Touadéra’s new term will hinge on promoting intercommunal dialogue in the south east, better integrating militias under army command, and reducing regional isolation through development and security reform. IRAN The falling value of Iran's national currency sparked demonstrations that since late December have grown into nationwide anti-regime unrest. The government has altered its subsidy policies but done little to dampen wider grievances. At least three dozen people have been killed as state forces crack down on protests that show little sign of slowing down. Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez says the Islamic Republic faces a major dilemma: it is neither willing nor able to adopt reforms that could meet expectations for political, social and economic change and on notice from U.S. President Donald Trump that outside intervention is possible if its repression intensifies. LEBANON Lebanon said it had passed a milestone in disarming Hizbollah, but the country’s fragile ceasefire deal with Israel remains imperilled. On Thursday, the Lebanese army announced that it had brought all weapons under state control in the southern area between the Litani River and the Israeli border. Israel immediately disputed the army’s assertion, saying Hizbollah retains military infrastructure in that region. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Beirut faces dangers ahead in any case. The army must soon move toward disarming Hizbollah north of the Litani, where the group refuses to comply – driving up the risk of internal discord. Yet Lebanese leaders also know that Israel will almost certainly respond to any hold-ups in disarming Hizbollah with severe military escalations, inflicting still more pain on their embattled country.
