Ten Challenges for the UN Even as the UN is mired in interlocking difficulties, the organisation can still contribute to conflict resolution and crisis management in many domains. The following list features countries and issue areas where the UN confronts either major challenges or opportunities in the year ahead. It is intended to demonstrate the myriad factors affecting how the UN and its member states respond to conflicts and emergencies around the world. The list is not exhaustive, however, and it excludes cases that Crisis Group has highlighted elsewhere or in years past, such as Afghanistan, the DRC, South Sudan, Ukraine and others. 1. Continuing UN engagement in southern Lebanon In August 2025, the U.S. and Israel strong-armed the Security Council into shutting down the UN peacekeeping mission in southern Lebanon (UNIFIL) – first established in 1978 and significantly upgraded by Resolution 1701 twenty years ago – by the end of 2026 (though the phased withdrawal of troops will extend considerably past 31 December). 50 “ Resolution 2790 ”, UNSC S/RES/2790, 28 August 2025. While questions about southern Lebanon have long vexed the Council, the latest conflagration between Israel and Hizbollah raises the stakes even higher. 51 Heiko Wimmen and David Wood, “ Entrenching a Meaningful Israel-Lebanon Ceasefire ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 19 June 2026. The danger is now that the UN will terminate its 48-year blue helmet operation without clarity on what kind of international presence, if any, might follow. Much will now depend on the trajectory of U.S.-backed negotiations between Israel and Lebanon, which to date have failed to produce a viable security arrangement. The two states signed a “framework agreement” on 26 June, under which the Lebanese army is to assert control of “pilot zones” in southern Lebanon, ensuring that Hizbollah no longer has a military footprint in these areas. 52 “ Trilateral Framework Between the United States of America, the State of Israel and the Republic of Lebanon ”, U.S. Department of State, 26 June 2026. Yet the scheme, which is meant to “serve as the mechanism for phased and verified (Israeli) redeployments”, has already run into trouble. 53 Ibid. Lebanon complains that Israel has kept attacking Lebanese territory, including with lethal airstrikes and the systematic destruction of villages, and authorised “pilot zones” only in areas that it never occupied. Israeli officials, for their part, make Hizbollah’s full disarmament a condition for the Israeli army’s withdrawal. 54 Maayan Lubell and Maya Gebeily, “ After US criticism, Israel ties Lebanon withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament ”, Reuters, 13 August 2026. Beirut officially outlawed Hizbollah’s military activities in March, but, in practice, it cannot risk trying to compel the group to disarm. 55 Lebanese political and military leaders have resisted calls to deploy the Lebanese army to confront Hizbollah by force. They fear that such a move could trigger disastrous domestic consequences, such as the military fracturing along sectarian lines. Crisis Group Middle East Briefing N°94, Containing Domestic Tensions in War-hit Lebanon , 27 February 2025. See also Michael Young, “ Pushing Beirut into an armed conflict with Hezbollah is insane ”, Diwan (blog), Carnegie Middle East Center, 14 May 2026. Even if the terms of the deal were to be spelled out more precisely, the belligerents would almost certainly refuse to sign up to the underlying bargain. Hizbollah rejects the direct Israel-Lebanon negotiations outright, insisting that Lebanon entrust Iran, the group’s patron, with securing a full Israeli withdrawal as part of Tehran’s negotiations with Washington. 56 “ Hezbollah insists on linking Lebanon to Iran-U.S. negotiations ”, Asharq al-Awsat , 13 July 2026. Though Israel has participated in the trilateral talks with Lebanon and the U.S., it refuses to accept another arrangement like Resolution 1701, under which its troops withdrew from Lebanon after the 2006 war while Hizbollah remained under arms. Debates about a future international presence will also be shaped by U.S. and Israeli scepticism. Israel has long questioned the value of UNIFIL in helping Lebanon constrain Hizbollah, and it has shown little appetite for a replacement that might obstruct its own military operations. The U.S. does not oppose an international mission per se, but it is wary of replicating a UNIFIL model that it deems ineffective. 57 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and UN officials, Beirut, July 2026. The U.S. and its Israeli partners have long argued that UNIFIL has failed to deter Hizbollah military operations south of the Litani River (even if it has no mandate to confront the militant group by force) and is too expensive. For background, see David Wood, “ Helping UNIFIL Restore Stability in Southern Lebanon ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 14 August 2025. Washington has sidelined the monitoring mechanism attached to the November 2024 ceasefire, in which UNIFIL and France (the Council’s penholder on Lebanon) were represented. Instead, an annex of the June framework agreement provides for a U.S.-headed “military coordination group”, through which Israel and Lebanon will manage tasks that UNIFIL or a successor force might have helped tackle, including “deconfliction, verification and overall implementation”. 58 The parties did not officially release this annex to the framework agreement, but they have not challenged the authenticity of a text leaked to the media in late June. “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, L’Orient Today , 29 June 2026. Other Council members and Lebanon strongly favour retaining an international presence, having reluctantly agreed to UNIFIL’s termination at the end of 2026 to avoid a U.S. veto that would have abruptly ended the mission in August 2025. 59 “ UN Interim Force in Lebanon: Vote on Final Mandate Renewal and Drawdown* ”, Security Council Report, 28 August 2025; Jamie Prentis, “ Lebanese MPs urge UN to extend peacekeeping mission ”, The National , 24 July 2026. The framework agreement does not mention the UN or Security Council resolution 1701. The annex, however, proposes a future role for a “mutually agreed-upon third-party entity” to verify that non-state armed groups have been cleared from each “pilot zone”. 60 “ The Lebanon-Israel ‘security’ annex agreement revealed ”, op. cit. To date, Israeli, Lebanese and U.S. negotiators have struggled to flesh out what such verification would entail, making it difficult for interested nations to commit troops to a mission that might prove dangerous. Yet even if the framework agreement eventually falls by the wayside, any other attempt to reach a deal that would link Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon and cessation of airstrikes with an end to Hizbollah attacks on Israel and disarmament of the group would in all likelihood hinge on some sort of third-party verification. International partners have begun debating options for a new multinational presence. In June, the Secretary-General proposed a follow-up UN mission involving both armed and unarmed troops. 61 The report, mandated by the Security Council in Resolution 2790, proposed three different deployment sizes: the largest option would entail 5,525 uniformed personnel, the middle one 3,370 and the lightest footprint approximately 1,980. See “ Letter dated 1 June 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/453, 1 June 2026. France and Italy have also announced plans to create a new multinational coalition in southern Lebanon as a successor to UNIFIL. 62 “ Lebanon president welcomes French, Italian efforts to form coalition to succeed UNIFIL ”, Arab News , 26 June 2026. In parallel, the European Union is weighing a separate mission comprising civilian and military personnel to advise and possibly train Lebanese forces – outside southern Lebanon – in addition to the €180 million it has already committed to support the Lebanese army. 63 Louay Faour, “ European powers seek greater role in south Lebanon’s post-war security architecture ”, The New Arab , 12 July 2026; Lili Bayer, “ EU diplomatic service proposes mission to train Lebanese forces, documents show ”, Reuters, 24 June 2026;“ European Peace Facility: Council adopts EUR 100 million assistance measure in support of the Lebanese Armed Forces ”, press release, Council of the EU, 4 June 2026. Any new multinational mission would have no choice but to work alongside the Lebanese-Israeli-U.S. security arrangement, even if that is not fully defined. Any new multinational mission would have no choice but to work alongside the Lebanese-Israeli-U.S. security arrangement, even if that is not fully defined. States wishing to participate in a mission would almost certainly demand Security Council authorisation prior to sending troops to southern Lebanon so as to guarantee their legal and political protection. Given U.S. veto power, Washington’s support on the Council remains indispensable, meaning that UN members cannot circumvent the trilateral mechanism championed by the Trump administration. Between now and the end of December, diplomats should monitor the evolution of security arrangements on the ground in southern Lebanon, while seeking to work out with Washington what kind of international deployment, if any, would be beneficial to Lebanon and its stability. It is unlikely that any security arrangement, whether the June framework agreement and/or some future deal, will either fully disarm Hizbollah or completely dissuade Israel from conducting military operations in Lebanon. But withdrawing UNIFIL, with no immediate successor in place, could leave a vacuum that makes an already tense situation even more volatile. By inheriting UNIFIL’s most valuable functions – in particular, monitoring and on-the-ground deconfliction – a new multinational mission could set up a guardrail against fresh escalation. Ideally, that force would eventually assume other roles in bolstering a sustainable security arrangement for southern Lebanon that becomes durable enough to stand on its own feet. 2. Adapting the UN’s political strategy for Sudan The UN continues to be on the margins of diplomacy aimed at halting Sudan’s devastating civil war. Secretary-General Guterres’ appointment of Pekka Haavisto as the new UN envoy in February has offered the organisation an opportunity to refresh its approach. Ramtane Lamamra – the UN’s previous diplomatic lead – struggled to find a bridge between the main warring parties, the Sudanese army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), or to coordinate the array of mediators working to resolve the conflict. The UN has had varying degrees of success in securing local deals over aid access, and it continues to prepare for a possible role in overseeing aspects of a mooted ceasefire. 64 See the Sudan entry in Crisis Group Briefing, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2025-2026 , op. cit. It is hard to see the UN leading efforts to stop the war, given the number of powerful foreign states backing the belligerents, but it should use the coming months to support other diplomatic tracks and raise global awareness of the urgent need to end the fighting. 65 “ Sudan: Closed Consultations ”, Security Council Report, 17 April 2026. Nearly eighteen months ago, UN officials acknowledged that Sudan’s plight had become the world’s largest humanitarian catastrophe. 66 “ UN Sudan Annual Results Report 2024 ”, UN Sudan, 4 June 2025. Conditions have only deteriorated since then. An independent UN panel determined that mass killings, rapes and other atrocities committed by the RSF in October 2025 in El Fasher, Darfur – the city that hosted the headquarters of the former UN peacekeeping operation UNAMID – were “indicators of a genocidal path”. 67 “ Sudan: Hallmarks of Genocide in El Fasher - Report of the Independent International Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR), UN Doc A/HRC/61/77, 19 February 2026. Diplomats and UN officials alike are sounding the alarm about similar risks in El-Obeid, North Kordofan. 68 “ Sudan: Imminent offensive on El Obeid must be halted – Türk warns of catastrophic impact on civilians ”, press release, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights, 18 June 2026; “ Joint Statement of G7 Foreign Ministers on El Obeid, Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, July 2026; “ Security Council Press Statement on Sudan (SC/16392) ”, UN Security Council, 20 June 2026. The two warring sides and their outside backers still believe there is more to gain from fighting than from negotiations. As matters stand, the country is in effect partitioned between the army and the RSF. 69 Crisis Group Africa Report N°211, Divided Sudan, Elusive Peace , 13 April 2026. To date, political negotiations have yielded few results. Much of the diplomatic focus has fallen on the Quad, a platform involving the U.S. and the three Arab powers with the most sway over the conflict parties – Egypt, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Its September 2025 roadmap, however, has won over neither belligerent, while Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, at loggerheads in conflict settings from Libya to Yemen, are doubling down on backing the army and RSF, respectively, stymying agreement within the Quad about what to do. 70 “ Joint Statement on Restoring Peace and Security in Sudan ”, U.S. Department of State, 12 September 2025; Comfort Ero and Alan Boswell, “ Latest Sudan Conference Shows Diplomacy is Backsliding ”, Crisis Group Analyst’s Notebook, 17 April 2026. In parallel, the UN is working alongside the African Union (AU), the EU, the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), a Horn of Africa body, and the Arab League to support Sudanese-led civilian political dialogues as part of a nascent diplomatic track called the Quintet; these mediators convened a meeting in Berlin in April and another in Addis Ababa two months later. 71 “ Sudan: Quintet Joint Statement on de-escalation of the conflict in Sudan ”, European External Action Service, 11 February 2026; “ Quintet Statement on Ongoing Consultations with Sudanese Political Actors ”, African Union, 6 June 2026. Sudanese participants cannot agree on how to move forward with the talks, however. Having completed an initial tour of Sudan and the region, Haavisto can begin revising the UN’s diplomatic strategy. 72 “ Pekka Haavisto (Personal Envoy of the Secretary-General for Sudan) on the situation in the country – Press Conference ”, Office of the UN Spokesperson, 25 June 2026. He will need to reassure all parties that the UN will be an independent, impartial counterpart, even though the army-led government is the legally recognised one in New York. Haavisto needs to build rapport with others across Sudan’s fragmented political spectrum, including armed, political and civil players that are enlisted in the war, on one side or the other, or are non-aligned, as well as the various African, Arab and other countries directly involved in the conflict in one way or another. He will also need to reach out to the RSF, even if its deeds have earned it widespread and deserved condemnation. Lamamra struggled to maintain this balance, with critics seeing him as weighting his engagements too heavily toward the army-led authorities and its allies. 73 Crisis Group interviews, opposition political figures; RSF officials and allies, October-November 2025. Haavisto now has a chance for a reset. Haavisto should also strengthen the UN’s contributions within the Quintet. He could begin by stepping up outreach to various civilian groups between official Quintet meetings, with a view to mending fences between them. He could also help institute more consistent interactions between the Quintet and the army-led government, which has so far proven reluctant to get involved with a political process that is independent of its authority and takes place outside the country. 74 “ Quintet Statement Ahead of Visit to Khartoum, the Republic of Sudan, 8-10 September ”, Delegation of the European Union to the African Union, 8 September 2026. The army is instead pursuing its own “national dialogue” inside Sudan, which few of its political or armed opponents look likely to join. Behind the scenes, the UN should ... search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts [in Sudan]. Behind the scenes, the UN should also search for opportunities to bolster and connect the two diplomatic coalitions driving peace efforts, neither of which appears to have momentum at present. One way forward would be for Haavisto to work closely with counterparts to quietly float proposals for how Sudan could be governed whenever the main belligerents and their outside patrons summon the political will to seek an end to the war. Haavisto could help communicate these proposals to Quad and Quintet members, the two warring parties, and Sudan’s other main political movements and figures. Though it is hard to imagine a breakthrough any time soon given the entrenched positions on both sides, the UN should separately continue planning for a possible role in backing humanitarian access and ceasefire arrangements between the army and RSF should regional support for peace efforts eventually rise. 75 The UN is not formal member of the Quad, but it has worked informally with the U.S. to scope out technicalities of a monitoring mechanism for the prospective humanitarian truce that was outlined in the Quad’s September 2025 roadmap. Lastly, the UN can redouble its efforts to draw world attention to Sudan’s war and humanitarian disaster, if nothing else to caution states about possible spillover. The next Secretary-General should make this task a priority – including by paying a solidarity visit to refugee camps in countries neighbouring Sudan – and also warn of the mounting risks to states in the Horn and Red Sea regions should the conflict fester. 76 Alan Boswell, “ As the Horn of Africa Nears Boiling Point, Time for Urgent Diplomacy ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 17 July 2026. The UN’s new leader should ensure that Haavisto and other UN envoys covering the Horn, central Africa and the Middle East remain in close contact in the hope of identifying opportunities to break the diplomatic deadlock among states in these areas. 3. Encouraging a role for the General Assembly in Gaza’s ceasefire Having repeatedly called for a ceasefire to halt Israel’s campaign against Hamas in Gaza from 2023-2025, the General Assembly has devoted little energy to discussing whether the mechanisms created to uphold it are working. The Security Council’s November 2025 endorsement of the Trump administration’s ceasefire plan in Resolution 2803 – including its highly unusual authorisation of a Trump-chaired Board of Peace to serve as Gaza’s transitional administration – has erected a de-facto firewall between the UN and the diplomatic apparatus overseeing the Palestinian enclave’s future, at least until the Board’s UN mandate expires at the end of 2027. 77 “Resolution 2803”, op. cit. With Gaza’s reconstruction at a virtual standstill and Israel tightening its grip on the territory, UN member states risk sitting idle as the U.S.-dominated Board veers further off course. 78 Crisis Group Middle East Report N°257, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , 24 August 2026. The Board’s backtracking on the terms of its own fifteen-point roadmap – which features a scheme for decommissioning Hamas’s weapons agreed to by Palestinian factions but opposed by Israel – is just one of many troubling developments. The Security Council is, unfortunately, unlikely to consider corrective action until the Board mandate’s 2027 sunset. In the interim, member states should at a minimum use the General Assembly to assess the Board’s performance and to catalyse diplomatic pressure for putting Gaza on track toward recovery and Palestinian statehood. The General Assembly was the hub of UN diplomatic activity on Gaza throughout the war, as both President Joe Biden and President Trump blocked the Security Council from taking meaningful action. UN members convened the Assembly’s Emergency Special Session on the Occupied Palestinian Territories (its dedicated format for discussing the broader conflict) on eight separate occasions, and they debated five failed Security Council resolutions. 79 The General Assembly debated the nine vetoed resolutions under a Liechtenstein-led veto initiative, established by the General Assembly in April 2022. For full list of General Assembly meetings convened under the veto initiative, see “ Living with the Veto ”, Security Council Report, 23 March 2026, p. 8. Member states adopted five major General Assembly decisions on various aspects of the conflict, including the New York Declaration of September 2025, which bolstered recognition of Palestinian statehood. 80 “ Admission of new Members to the United Nations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/23, 10 May 2024; Advisory Opinion of the International Court of Justice ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/24, 19 September 2024; “ Support for the mandate of the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/25, 16 December 2024; “ Protection of civilians and upholding legal and humanitarian obligations ”, UNGA A/RES/ES-10/27, 13 June 2025; “ Endorsement of the New York Declaration on the Peaceful Settlement of the Question of Palestine and the Implementation of the Two-State Solution ”, UNGA A/80/L.1/Rev.1, 10 September 2025. Unless something changes, they will remain under siege, subject to bombardment and denied a future until the Board of Peace decides that Hamas has met Israel’s demands. Washington would likely veto any Security Council action perceived to criticise Israel – which receives unconditional backing from the U.S. at the UN – or to cast doubt on the legitimacy and efficacy of Trump’s peace efforts. But that ought not to be a justification for inaction in the General Assembly or elsewhere. UN members should use the General Assembly to challenge the Board of Peace’s unhelpful domination of the diplomatic space. The next meeting of the Global Alliance for the Two-State Solution, scheduled for September, could kickstart that endeavour. These platforms provide an opportunity to reaffirm the necessity of the UN-led aid distribution network in Gaza, which remains the most capable one in the strip. See Ed Miliband, “ Foreign Secretary Oral Statement on Israel-Palestine ”, speech to UK Parliament, 8 September 2026. For background, see Crisis Group Report, Hollow Promises: Resetting Gaza’s Ceasefire , op. cit. Reinforcing security and justice support to Haiti International efforts to help restore security in Haiti have reached a decisive phase. The Gang Suppression Force (GSF), a multilateral mission authorised by the Security Council in September 2025 and backed with UN logistical support, landed in Haiti in June. 87 “ Resolution 2793 ”, UNSC S/RES/2793, 30 September 2025. Expected to be at full strength by the end of the year, the force faces the daunting task of confronting armed gangs that have held much of the country hostage for years. 88 Crisis Group Report, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , op. cit.; “ Situation of human rights in Haiti ”, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights A/HRC/61/74, 23 March 2026. International efforts to staff, fund and equip the GSF are essential to ending this painful chapter in Haiti’s history. But even if this force puts gangs on the back foot, it will only be the start of a far longer campaign to bring peace to the country. Haiti’s government and international partners should work closely with the UN to build exit ramps for individuals willing to abandon the gangs and reinforce new judicial bodies to investigate and prosecute gang crimes. The GSF’s close working relationship with the UN could help it avoid the problems that plagued its predecessor, the Kenyan-led Multinational Security Support mission. A new UN support office services the force’s logistics needs (ranging from supplying rations and fuel to covering its medical services and constructing bases) and channels monetary contributions its way. 89 “ Budgets for the periods from 1 October 2025 to 30 June 2026 and from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027 for the United Nations Support Office in Haiti ”, UNGA A/80/630, 10 February 2026. Reasonably predictable funding from the UN’s assessed budget has enabled eight countries to pledge enough troops to surpass the initial target of 5,500 personnel, though as of publication only around 1,200 troops are on the ground. 90 As of publication, the GSF included personnel sent from Chad, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Mongolia and Sri Lanka. A separate UN trust fund has nearly $226 million in voluntary donations, which have been promised to cover the wages of deployed personnel. 91 As of 30 June, the Trust Fund had $233 million in total pledges, with $184 million in cash receipts. The UN had spent approximately $67 million of the cash receipts leaving $117 million in hand. “ Contributions to the Trust Fund for the Multinational Security Support (MSS) mission for Haiti authorised under SCR 2699 (2023) and Gang Suppression Force (GSF) authorised under SCR 2793 ”, UN, 13 July 2026; “ United Nations Integrated Office in Haiti: Report of the Secretary-General ”, UNSC S/2026/574, 14 July 2026, p. 10. Informal ties also reinforce the force’s partnership with the UN. The Standing Group of Partners, the ad hoc political body with the job of overseeing the mission, appointed UN peacekeeping veterans to the force’s highest ranking civilian and uniformed positions. 92 The Standing Group of Partners includes the U.S., Canada, El Salvador, Guatemala, Jamaica, Kenya, and the Bahamas. “ Special representative named for U.S. backed-Gang Suppression Force in Haiti ”, Miami Herald , 2 December 2025; “ UN-appointed anti-gang force commander arrives in Haiti to lead expanded mission ”, Haitian Times , 15 May 2026. These officials are coordinating with senior staff in BINUH, the UN political office in Haiti tasked with engaging Haitian counterparts on governance and human rights, and in the force’s logistics support office. The UN headquarters gave wide-ranging assistance to the force as it went about its technical preparations, including by helping prepare its concept of operations and carry out pre-deployment training. 93 Crisis Group interviews, diplomats and UN officials, New York and Port-au-Prince, February, April and June 2026. Difficulties will inevitably arise once the GSF begins going after the gangs in earnest. Civilians are at risk of becoming collateral damage once the mission launches offensives. 94 The Multinational Security Support mission, by contrast, never mustered more than 1,000 police personnel, struggled to secure funding and battled the gangs only alongside the national police. Troop-contributing countries that have taken part in previous UN peacekeeping operations will need to ensure that the soldiers they send to Haiti are prepared for a hostile environment. Any gains will be short-lived if Haiti and its partners do not take steps to dismantle the criminal groups for good. Once the force reaches full capacity, member states hope that it can quickly impose a modicum of security. 96 Crisis Group Report, Undoing Haiti’s Deadly Gang Alliance , op. cit. But any gains will be short-lived if Haiti and its partners do not take steps to dismantle the criminal groups for good. Offering individuals the opportunity to leave the gangs safely, with support for new livelihoods through a program of disarmament, dismantlement and reintegration, will be critical for winding down these groups. 97 The Haitian government and the UN do not use the more common term “demobilisation”, which refers to dissolving non-state armed groups as defined under international humanitarian law. Instead, they refer to “dismantlement”, which envisages individual rather than collective action. “ Letter dated 29 May 2026 from the Secretary-General addressed to the President of the Security Council ”, UNSC S/2026/449, 29 May 2026, p. 3. Preserving UN operations in the Central African Republic UN peacekeepers have been at the forefront of international efforts to protect civilians and back peace initiatives in the Central African Republic (CAR) since first being dispatched to the country in 2014. The U.S. and China, two of the Council’s permanent members, have suggested that the mission, known as MINUSCA, should now begin preparing to exit, citing the progress the country has made toward stability. (Their own interest is to lower the cost of UN peacekeeping.) Elections held in late December 2025 without a major disruption may bolster their case. 103 Charles Bouëssel, “ Central African Republic: Consolidating Security Gains after the Elections ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 27 January 2026. But when renewing MINUSCA’s mandate in November, diplomats should ensure that the mission retains sufficient capacity to protect civilians and deter armed groups in the country’s troubled east, since it is the only entity that can provide a buffer against worsening instability in that region. MINUSCA continues to fill gaps that the Central African authorities cannot plug. A guarantor of the 2019 peace agreement, the UN mission oversees local peace dialogues and disarmament programs across the country. 104 The Union for Peace in the Central African Republic, Return, Reclamation and Rehabilitation and the Patriotic Movement for the Central African Republic are the most prominent armed groups participating in these disarmament programs. See: “ The Situation in the Central African Republic ”, UNSC S/2026/494, 15 June 2026, paras 8-10. Though CAR’s allies – Rwanda and Russian paramilitaries from the Wagner Group – helped Bangui regain control of towns across the country after a 2021 rebel offensive, MINUSCA is the only external partner tasked with protecting civilians from violence. In many areas outside the capital Bangui, local institutions depend on the mission to build and repair government offices, supply logistical assistance and offer physical protection. The threat of insurgency in CAR is much lower than it was a few years ago, but pockets of insecurity persist along the country’s eastern borders. 105 Bouëssel, “ Central African Republic: Consolidating Security Gains after the Elections ”, op. cit. Fighters from the ex-Séléka rebel coalition, which seized power in 2013 and plunged the country into civil war, as well as allied militias are active in the north east, most recently attacking CAR state forces and UN peacekeepers on 30 June in Am-Dafock, on the Sudan border. 106 “ Central African Republic Situation Report No. 74 as of 30 June, 2026 ”, UN OCHA, 2 July 2026; “ MINUSCA strongly condemns the attack against Am Dafock and the firing targeting the Mission’s base ”, press release, UN OCHA, 30 June 2026. Separately, the Zandé self-defence militia based in Haut-Mbomou prefecture, in the south east, continue to assail civilians and state forces. 107 Crisis Group Africa Report N°319, Central African Republic: Reining in the Zandé Militia , 20 November 2025. UN peacekeepers are often the only force capable of deterring or responding to urgent threats [in the Central African Republic]. Intercommunal violence, opportunistic crime and conflicts between nomadic herders and sedentary farmers remain prevalent nationwide. 108 Crisis Group Africa Report N°317, Violence and Herding in the Central African Republic: Time to Act , 28 May 2025. Women and girls are vulnerable to rape in many places as a result. Spillover from Sudan’s civil war exacerbates these risks: Central African rebels have become war entrepreneurs, providing fighters for both the RSF and the Sudanese army in exchange for money, while over 40,000 Sudanese refugees have fled into north-eastern CAR. UN peacekeepers are often the only force capable of deterring or responding to urgent threats. These developments should give Council members pause when they are considering a drawdown for MINUSCA. In November 2025, the U.S. pushed the Council to task the mission with charting an exit strategy ahead of the mandate renewal, owing in part to their assessment of CAR’s improved conditions and their scepticism about renewing UN operations indefinitely. 109 A draft is expected to be circulated by 15 September. “ Resolution 2800 ”, UNSC S/RES/2800, para 48; “ Central African Republic: Vote on MINUSCA’s Mandate Renewal ”, Security Council Report, 12 November 2025. U.S. and Chinese diplomats have found common cause in lobbying for reductions to the mission’s budget. 110 Crisis Group interviews, UN diplomats, New York, November 2025. Separately, the UN’s liquidity crisis has already forced the mission to repatriate nearly 4,000 troops (more than one quarter of the total) and close 21 operating bases that allowed MINUSCA to intervene in a range of conflict-affected areas outside Bangui. 111 UN leaders used the financial constraints as motivation to reposition MINUSCA personnel in a more mobile posture to get the most out of the smaller footprint. While the Court’s critics tend to disparage it as feckless, it serves an important function in reinforcing and applying international legal rules relating to mass violence. While the Court’s critics tend to disparage it as feckless, it serves an important function in reinforcing and applying international legal rules relating to mass violence. It keeps the prospect of accountability on the table even in situations where the ability to enforce its decisions is limited. 129 Crisis Group Briefing, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Security , op. cit. Its diminution is likely to erode the force of international humanitarian law yet further. The Court’s member states should work together to limit the damage. While they may not be the world’s most powerful, there is strength in their numbers. They should encourage states that are vulnerable to U.S. pressure to stay the course and do what they can to buttress the Court’s resiliency. At a practical level, countries could offer basic banking services to ICC officials who have been targeted by U.S. sanctions. Member states should also use their negotiations of the annual General Assembly resolution on the ICC, scheduled to take place between October and November, to drum up public support for its work and galvanise pushback against the U.S. attack on this pillar of the international justice architecture. 7. Recalibrating UN operations in Myanmar Myanmar’s installation of a nominally civilian administration in April, following elections stage-managed by the military four months earlier, has created a dilemma for the UN. The elections have not restored state authority or legitimacy, and Naypyitaw does not have a credible strategy for ending the country’s armed conflict, either through negotiation or military victory. 130 Crisis Group Asia Briefing N°188, Myanmar’s New Administration: Military Consolidation, Not Transition , 3 June 2026. Humanitarian conditions continue to deteriorate as fighting, economic decline and fear of conscription grip the country. 131 “ Myanmar Humanitarian Update no. 51 ”, UN OCHA, 9 March 2026. Even so, more of Myanmar’s regional neighbours are giving the new administration de facto recognition, with Min Aung Hlaing – the coup leader who is now president – recently visiting India, China, Laos, Thailand and Vietnam. Beijing maintains a firm position limiting discussion of Myanmar at the UN, while Secretary-General Guterres has shown little willingness to invest political capital in the issue. Absent new diplomatic momentum in the near term, UN officials will need to calibrate engagement carefully to reduce harm, sustain livelihoods and support development without conferring legitimacy on abusive forms of rule. Much of this work will fall to the new UN leadership in Yangon. In October 2025, Guterres appointed veteran official Gwyn Lewis as resident and humanitarian coordinator ad interim, ending the ineffective practice of rotating the position among agency heads. 132 Lewis has the ad interim designation because the Secretary-General does not want to acknowledge the authorities politically by writing to seek their agreement to the appointment. See Crisis Group Special Briefing N°12, Ten Challenges for the UN in 2024-2025 , 10 September 2024. The resident coordinator will need to shape the UN’s engagement with the new administration while ensuring the organisation can continue delivering essential humanitarian and development assistance. Just as importantly, the office should provide clear strategic direction to the whole UN country team so that agencies operate according to a consistent approach within current political constraints. UN officials will also need to manage relations with Myanmar’s ethnic armed groups. Aid agencies already deliver assistance in parts of the country outside state control, working through local partners despite the absence of formal agreements with Naypyitaw. As the devastating March 2025 earthquake showed, the UN remains one of the few organisations capable of delivering international aid at scale to civilians in much of the country, including areas outside government control. 133 Richard Horsey, “ Support Vital for Myanmar’s Quake Victims, Despite Military Obstacles ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 1 April 2025; “ End of Mission Report United Nations Disaster Assessment & Coordination – Earthquake 7.7M Response – Myanmar (29Mar-16Apr 2025) ”, UN OCHA, 23 February 2026; “ First person: Myanmar aid workers brave conflict and harsh conditions to bring aid to earthquake victims ”, UN, 30 April 2025. The World Bank and the Asian Development Bank have become the largest and most consistent providers of assistance to Myanmar’s people, but they rightly cannot channel funds through a government they do not recognise. Their support is therefore delivered off-budget – outside state systems – and depends on UN agencies for fiduciary oversight and distribution. The resident coordinator will need to mind the political sensitivities of the UN role in providing this support, as well as the differing approaches of neighbouring states – including Bangladesh, China, India and Thailand – toward informal cross-border assistance. 134 Thomas Kean, “ Time to Reset Bangladesh’s Approach to the Rohingya ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 8 July 2026; Crisis Group Asia Briefing N°186, Fractured Heartland: Shan Politics and Conflict in Post-coup Myanmar , 27 November 2025. The next Secretary-General will have an opportunity to reset the UN’s overall strategy [in Myanmar] and provide stronger political backing for the envoy. The same balancing act applies to the UN’s diplomatic track. Special Envoy Julie Bishop, who has struggled to translate her high-level regional access into meaningful entry points for UN diplomacy, has burned most of her bridges with Myanmar’s leaders by taking an increasingly strident public line – for example, returning from Naypyitaw to tell UN member states in June that the election was designed to entrench military rule and that Min Aung Hlaing’s proposed 100-day peace plan inspires no confidence. 135 “Special Envoy on Myanmar’s remarks to the General Assembly”, UN Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, 19 June 2026. The next Secretary-General will have an opportunity to reset the UN’s overall strategy and provide stronger political backing for the envoy. 136 The envoy role was mandated by the UN General Assembly in December 2017 to support UN engagement on a range of political priorities. “ Situation of human rights in Myanmar ”, UN General Assembly, UN Doc. A/RES/72/248, 23 January 2018. An important test will come at the UN General Assembly. Since the 2021 coup, China and the U.S. have informally maintained the status quo by leaving in place the incumbent ambassador, Kyaw Moe Tun, who was appointed by the elected government and later aligned himself with the parallel National Unity Government. Naypyitaw is expected to press its case to have its nominee recognised as Myanmar’s permanent representative when the Credentials Committee meets in November. China committed in a 17 June statement with Min Aung Hlaing in Beijing to support Myanmar’s “full, equal and constructive participation” at the UN, repeating this formula in the General Assembly two days later. 137 “ Joint Statement of the Republic of the Union of Myanmar and the People’s Republic of China on Accelerating the Building of a China – Myanmar Community with a Shared Future (17 June 2026) ”, Republic of the Union of Myanmar, 18 June 2026; and informal meeting of the General Assembly plenary convened to hear the Special Envoy’s briefing on Myanmar, 19 June 2026. It is unclear what diplomatic capital Beijing may expend to this end. A decision has been put off each year because the permanent members who sit on the Credentials Committee – China, the U.S. and Russia – have preferred the status quo to a divisive vote, and because any consideration of the competing credentials for Myanmar could prompt a similar debate about the Taliban authorities in Afghanistan. 138 The Committee, appointed at the General Assembly’s first plenary meeting under rule 28, met once in the 80th session, on 25 November 2025. Its report proposed a single postponement of the competing credentials for both Myanmar and Afghanistan, adopted without a vote. See “Report of the Credentials Committee”, A/80/547, 25 November 2025, paras 8 to 10, approved by the General Assembly on 12 December 2025 (Resolution 80/114). The credentials debate could coincide with the International Court of Justice’s expected ruling in the genocide case against Myanmar that was filed by The Gambia. 139 Public hearings in The Gambia v. Myanmar case closed at the International Court of Justice on 29 January 2026, and judgment is pending. The Court will rule both on whether Myanmar committed genocide and on whether it failed to prevent and punish genocidal acts. A finding that Myanmar committed genocide would be the first time the Court has held a state responsible for such a crime. In the two previous genocide judgments, Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro and Croatia v. Serbia , the Court found a failure to prevent and punish in the first and no proven specific intent in the second. See “The concluding stage of The Gambia v. Myanmar genocide case before the International Court of Justice”, Global Centre for the Responsibility to Protect, 10 February 2026. Although the case’s outcome remains uncertain, a finding of state responsibility arriving at the same time as a credentials dispute would intensify international divisions over the issue of the Myanmar administration’s legitimacy. It would also narrow even further the UN’s room for manoeuvre in Myanmar, since Naypyitaw would view it with even more antagonism. The cost for regional leaders of associating with Min Aung Hlaing might rise as well, complicating high-level visits to the country though probably not turning the tide on diplomatic normalisation. The UN does not have the leverage to achieve major change in Myanmar. But the organisation is crucial for delivering humanitarian and other support to vulnerable civilians. A credible operational strategy, backed by sustained political support from headquarters, will therefore remain essential to efforts to alleviate public hardship and the effects of armed conflict. 8. Protecting the UN’s gender work in conflict settings The UN’s reform agenda has raised thorny issues about how the institution should organise its work to support women and girls. In late 2025, Secretary-General Guterres proposed merging the UN Population Fund (UNFPA) with UN Women as part of the UN80 initiative. 140 Other proposed mergers under UN80 include combining the UN Development Programme and the UN Office for Project Services; the UN Institute for Training and Research and the UN System Staff College; and the World Health Organisation and the Joint United Nations Programme on HIV/AIDS. UNFPA leads the UN’s work on sexual and reproductive health, while UN Women (approximately one third the size of UNFPA) advocates for normative shifts on gender issues, including the Women, Peace and Security (WPS) agenda, and distributes funding to NGOs for related programming. 141 With an annual budget of $1.53 billion, UNFPA’s model focuses on service delivery through 3,569 staff in 150 countries. “ As-Is Analysis: A Baseline for the UNFPA - UN Women Strategic Merger Assessment ”, UN80 Initiative, Work Package 4, Working Document, 6 March 2026. Whether the merger will come to pass is not clear. Amid aid cuts and pushback against gender equality worldwide, many member states and UN officials worry that combining these entities would hobble the UN’s work on gender, including efforts to support women and girls affected by conflict, for years to come. The Secretary-General’s proposal included a request for a UN-prepared report (published in March) that evaluated the risks and benefits of a merger – an idea that had been discussed and discarded in 2023. 142 Member states and UN officials report a sense that, whatever its findings, the study was meant to recommend a merger because the Secretary-General and Deputy Secretary-General wished to show that they were serious about making large-scale reforms to make the UN more efficient. For more, see “ Independent Review of the UN System’s Capacity to Deliver on Gender Equality ”, Dalberg, 11 February 2023. The merger it proposed would bring together UNFPA and UN Women in a new entity with a unified voice. It would also save the UN between $32 and $38 million per year, which the UN would urge member states to reinvest in the new entity’s work. 143 “ Preliminary Findings from the Strategic Merger Assessment of UNFPA and UN Women ”, UN80 Initiative, 30 March 2026. The assessment acknowledged, but did not suggest ways to mitigate, the risk that member states could eliminate important but contentious areas of work – including a number of sexual and reproductive health services and work on LGBTQI+ protections – during negotiations to create the new entity. 144 Given that the U.S. has been spearheading the pressure on the Secretary-General and his deputy to show their willingness to streamline the UN, combined with U.S. positions against the UN’s gender equality and WPS, many member states and UN officials point out that this merger proposal is like offering the U.S. a prime opportunity to weaken the UN’s gender work for years to come, by opening a negotiation on a new mandate where no negotiation or new mandate is necessary or desirable. [The] separate mandates [of UN Women and UNFPA] help the UN respond to distinct political, security and humanitarian issues. There are other risks, too. Though both agencies work on gender issues in conflict-affected countries, their separate mandates help the UN respond to distinct political, security and humanitarian issues. 145 In 2025, UNFPA was active in efforts to ameliorate 50 humanitarian crises, while in 2024 UN Women was working in 43. See “ 2026 Humanitarian Action Overview ”, UNFPA, April 2026; and “ Humanitarian Action Annual Report 2024”, UN Women, 2025. In Afghanistan, for example, UNFPA runs programs including menstrual health education and support for midwives, all in compliance with Taliban edicts. 146 “ Youth centre provides life-changing menstrual hygiene information and supplies to Afghan girls ”, UNFPA Afghanistan, 28 May 2026. Though interactions between the Taliban and UNFPA personnel are sometimes “tense”, the authorities recognise the need for the agency’s services. 147 Crisis Group interview, UN official, New York, July 2026. UN Women’s Afghanistan office is on shakier ground. The Taliban consider UN Women to be among their loudest critics and reject the agency’s frequent calls for repealing highly restrictive decrees as interference in Afghanistan’s internal affairs. 148 Mohammad Farshad Daryosh, “ Potzel criticizes bans on women, girls in Afghanistan ”, Tolo News, 8 March 2023; “ IEA-MOFA statement regarding SRSG briefing to UNSC ”, press release, 22 June 2023. While UN Women supports livelihood projects that the Taliban see as consistent with their goals of keeping the economy afloat and help the agency maintain an in-country presence, its normative positions are a persistent source of friction. Combining the two UN entities may have the effect of imputing these positions to UNFPA and create unnecessary risks for the latter. 149 “ Empowering Afghan Women and Energizing Economies ”, UN Women Afghanistan, 2025. UN efforts to support more than one million Rohingya refugees from Myanmar living in Cox’s Bazar, Bangladesh, also show why keeping UN Women and UNFPA separate is helpful in providing support for women and girls affected by conflict. 150 Kean, “ Time to Reset Bangladesh’s Approach to the Rohingya ”, op. cit. UNFPA offers health services in response to prevalent sexual violence and high pregnancy rates. It must be politically adroit in its engagement with Bangladeshi authorities, given local sensitivities around sexual and reproductive health. 151 Crisis Group telephone interview, humanitarian health practitioner, 25 June 2024. See also Cristal Downing, “ Amid Aid Cuts, a Renewed U.S. Policy Increases Health Risks for Women and Girls in Conflict Areas ”, Crisis Group Commentary, 3 March 2025. By contrast, UN Women supports women refugees (including through vocational training) and is involved in politically complex conversations with Dhaka about supporting eventual refugee return to Myanmar. 152 Kean, “ Time to Reset Bangladesh’s Approach to the Rohingya ”, op. cit. Currently, the conversations about health care and political matters are separate, so if the two need to raise their issues with authorities at similar times they can do so separately – even if in coordination – without having to choose one topic over the other. UN officials worry that the appointment of a single UN interlocutor to coordinate with the authorities on both immediate humanitarian priorities and longer-term political objectives could pit the new organisation’s teams against each other when deciding which issues should take higher priority in senior-level engagement. 153 The merger assessment considers this single interlocutor model to be a strength of the proposal, but UN officials consider it a weakness because of the potential trade-offs that would have to be made internally when deciding the priorities to be addressed in government engagement. Crisis Group interviews, UN officials, January-July 2026. Member states across the geographic and political spectrum have expressed concerns about the proposed merger. A coalition including Canada, Poland, South Korea and Sweden – which includes top contributors to both agencies – wrote to the Secretary-General saying they were “not in a position to support such a proposal” given the lack of clarity on how the two mandates could be safeguarded. 154 Canada letter to the UN Secretary-General , 15 May 2026. Separately, Russia and China also emphasised the need to protect the two mandates, albeit voicing different concerns. Russia pointed out that member states have no agreed-upon definition of “sexual rights”, saying it is therefore “inappropriate” for the proposed new entity to work in this domain. China, for its part, stressed that the process of merging two entities should be member state-led and transparent, suggesting that it objected to how the recommendation came about. 155 For more, see Letter from Russia to the UN Secretary-General , UNGA A/80/710, 20 April 2026; Remarks by China on the UN80 initiative , 8 June 2026. In response to requests from member state governing boards for alternative proposals, UN Women and UNFPA distributed their own papers, first in June and then in August, suggesting ways to align some of their work without a merger, including through shared data analytics and joint projects on gender-based violence in some locations. 156 The second of these papers also went into further detail on the costs of a merger, including the initial four-year financial impact ranging from a $9.9 million loss to a $38.2 million gain, after which savings could reach $35.1 million, depending on transition costs and organisational design. According to the UN’s own assessment of the merger, savings would be reinvested in the new entity. “ Further evidence and analysis on both the merger scenario and on alternative options to enhance alignment, impact and efficiency”, UN Women/UNFPA, 7 August 2026. Member states and UN officials should consider whether these proposals would satisfy the desire to increase efficiency without risking the mandate dilution implied by a merger. In so doing, they should shy away from politically ill-timed proposals that would threaten hard-won gains and could weaken UN support for women and girls in conflict and other crises in the long term. 9. Recasting discussions of the future of UN peace operations Diplomats routinely cite peace operations as one of the UN’s flagship contributions to peace and security. But the Security Council has not authorised a large-scale blue helmet force for over a decade, and the number of troops and police personnel serving under the organisation’s banner has halved in the same period. There have also been few new UN Special Political Missions (SPMs), which are solely or largely civilian in nature. As noted in the introduction, the Trump administration has pushed for budget cuts to UN missions of all kinds, questioning their expense, efficiency and apparent lack of concrete goals. To guide discussions about how to revitalise this atrophying tool, the Secretary-General published a review of all forms of peace operations. 157 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations: report of the Secretary General ”, UN General Assembly A/80/798 – UN Security Council S/2026/600, 22 July 2026. The review came out in August, having originally been requested by member states in late 2024. Though this study covers political missions – and makes a strong pitch for the UN to reinvest in prevention and good offices, discussed in the next section – many of its more technical recommendations are specific to operations with military and police components. A number of UN members, including the U.S., have complained that it says nothing startlingly new. 158 See, for example, “ The future of United Nations peace operations: Implementation of the recommendations of the High-level Independent Panel on Peace Operations ”, UNGA A/70/357 – UNSC S/2015/682, 2 September 2015; “ Declaration of Shared Commitments on UN Peacekeeping Operations ”, UN Secretary-General, 16 August 2018; “ The Pact For The Future ”, UN General Assembly A/RES/79/1, 22 September 2024, paras 42(a)-42(g); “ Chair’s Summary – UN Peacekeeping Ministerial 2025 ”, 14 May 2025. But it is a solid overview of the challenges facing UN operations and a starting point for diplomatic discussions of solving them. UN missions face new challenges like disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks for which they are ill prepared. The report’s diagnosis of the problems facing peace operations is hard to dispute. As it notes, the UN is often tasked with propping up weak ceasefires and political processes amid endemic violence. UN missions face new challenges like disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks for which they are ill prepared. A divided and distracted Security Council provides limited political support for UN personnel on the ground and does not update their mandates in a timely fashion when they encounter changing threats (Council diplomats admit this judgment is fair). 159 “ Provisional Verbatim of the 10,137th Meeting of the UN Security Council ”, UNSC S/PV.10137, 15 April 2026. The Secretary-General stakes out a series of sensible, albeit technocratic, responses to these issues. He suggests that the Security Council should direct UN operations to find political approaches to ending and mitigating conflict; work out “compacts” with states defining shared commitments to making missions work; and take a flexible approach to reviewing and revising mandates. His paper calls for a further Secretariat report examining the capabilities UN missions need to become more agile, while hammering home the need for missions to become more cost-effective and accountable for their performance. UN staffers and diplomats will spend much of the year ahead following up on these proposals, but even if they can fix some of the process issues, broader political questions about the future of UN peace operations will remain. In today’s fraught geopolitical environment, the space for mediators – hailing from the UN or elsewhere – to craft sustainable peace processes will likely remain limited. 160 Crisis Group Briefing, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Security , op. cit. Embattled governments in regions such as the Sahel and countries like Haiti want international forces to neutralise their opponents rather than coax them to the negotiating table. Guterres and most UN officials agree that as a rule the UN should not become directly involved in peace enforcement, even if the Security Council backs ad hoc missions like the GSF in Haiti that the UN system can support logistically and administratively. The fundamental challenge facing the UN is to rebuild a case for conflict parties and other actors to invest in mediation processes and peacebuilding efforts that minimise violence, and that UN peace operations are qualified to offer these efforts support when useful. There may be an audience for this argument. As Crisis Group has noted, efforts to crush insurgencies through force alone in cases such as the Sahel have gone awry. 161 Crisis Group Africa Report N°314, Northern Mali: Returning to Dialogue , 20 February 2024; Crisis Group Africa Report N°321, Understanding JNIM’s Expansion Beyond the Sahel , 20 February 2026; Crisis Group Briefing, Causes of Peace in an Era of Hard Security , op. cit. While the UN still has a lot of work to do improving how peace operations work, Guterres leaves them with a helpful to-do list. The next Secretary-General’s overarching challenge will be restoring the organisation’s standing as an actor that can deploy peace operations to backstop other peace initiatives when they show promise. 10. Repositioning the Secretary-General’s approach to crisis management When the next Secretary-General takes office on 1 January 2027, she or he will have a brief window of opportunity to overhaul the UN Secretariat’s strategy-making and crisis response mechanisms. Incoming UN leaders typically shake up their executive offices in their first months and table broader proposals for reorganising the Secretariat for member states to consider. 162 Thomas Weiss and Tatiana Carayannis, “ Windows of Opportunity for UN Reform: Historical Insights for the Next Secretary-General ”, International Affairs , vol. 93, no. 2 (2017). In the course of selecting a new Secretary-General, member states have emphasised that the winner should concentrate on peace and security. Many candidates have promised to engage on crisis diplomacy personally, a point emphasised in Guterres’ review of all forms of peace operations. 163 “ Review on the future of all forms of United Nations peace operations: report of the Secretary General ”, op. cit., paras 24-29. But it is necessary to improve the institution’s systems for generating policy options for dealing with new and persistent conflicts, which have grown rusty in recent years. They will also have to prepare for the fall-out of global risks like the El Niño climate pattern on conflict affected states, which will test the diplomatic, humanitarian and development arms of the UN system. Though Secretary-General Guterres made streamlining the UN’s peace and security pillar an early priority, organisational glitches have proliferated on his watch. 164 For more, see proposed budget for 2018-2019 related to the peace and security reform , UNGA A/72/772, 1 March 2018. Guterres has kept a tight grip on decision-making. Officials dealing with peace operations and political affairs, whether in New York or around the world, often feel out of the loop. As crises have proliferated, senior decision-makers in the Secretariat have become debilitatingly cautious, and inter-departmental turf wars (a perennial feature of life at the UN) have festered. Security Council members complain that when they ask for options papers from the Secretary-General – as they have done in cases including Gaza, Sudan, Haiti and Lebanon – the results come slowly and are generally mediocre at best. 165 Forti, “ Prioritising Peace: What the UN Should Ask of Its Next Secretary-General ”, op. cit. UN officials agree that a high priority for the next Secretary-General is to sort out [the] option-generating and decision-making mess. UN officials agree that a high priority for the next Secretary-General is to sort out this option-generating and decision-making mess. Some believe it is a matter of a change in culture (and, in some cases, personnel). Others argue that it is necessary to centralise the UN’s systems for producing options and crisis coordination in a new planning cell inside the Secretary-General’s office, to speed up the process of responding to new conflicts and Security Council requests for help. The next Secretary-General would be well advised to resolve this top-level wiring issue – which will require fairly slight budgetary and managerial effort – before embarking on any wider reform of the Secretariat’s Departments of Peace Operations and Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, which will require more extensive inter-governmental negotiations, and more battles over turf. The new Secretary-General’s choice of senior officials dealing with peace and security will also come under scrutiny. The veto powers typically insist on inserting nominees to run significant departments, often as bargains during the final stages of choosing the Secretary-General. An unwritten division among the major powers has emerged: France fills the post of Under Secretary-General for Peace Operations, the U.S. takes political affairs, the UK deals with humanitarian affairs, China handles economic and social affairs, and Russia names the head of the Office of Counter-terrorism. UN officials and other member states grumble about this carve-up, but successive Secretaries-General have concluded that it is a political necessity to gain support from the Council’s permanent members. 166 Thant Myint-U, “ The Next Secretary-General, Secretariat Reform and the Vexed Question of Senior Appointments ”, NYU Center on International Cooperation, 11 April 2016. Some Secretariat staff worry that the Trump administration will lobby for a hardline loyalist to oversee the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, undermining the Secretary-General’s authority. While it may not be possible to ignore the veto powers entirely, however, both Guterres and his predecessor Ban Ki-moon were able to resist appointing nominees from Washington, Paris and London whom they deemed unsuitable. 167 Ben Donaldson and Fred Carver, “ Backroom Deals: The trade in promises for support between member states and candidates for UN Secretary-General ”, 1 for 8 Billion/Platforma CIPÓ, June 2026. To show at least a modicum of autonomy, the next Secretary-General should follow suit, potentially asking the veto powers for informal shortlists of candidates for particular roles. Equally or more importantly, she or he should look for strong appointees from non-veto capitals to fill key posts in the executive office – including Deputy Secretary-General, Chief of Staff and Political Director – who can buttress top-level decision-making and help balance the influence of P5 proxies in internal debates. 168 Daniel Safran-Hon, “ The Next Secretary-General’s First Decision: Who Runs the 38th Floor? ”, IPI Global Observatory, 13 May 2026. These senior officials could take on direct mediation roles as well. 169 Daniel Safran-Hon, “ UN Peacemaking Needs More Diplomats, Not More Doctrine ”, IPI Global Observatory, 26 August 2026. For all the qualities of her or his advisers, the Secretary-General will also need to get personally involved directly in conflict prevention efforts and peace processes. The new Secretary-General’s team will need to set up a series of early visits for the boss to key capitals in various regions so that she or he can signal that the UN is reinvesting in the business of conflict management. Whereas Guterres was discouraged by early failures in his peacemaking efforts, his successor should embrace a more persistent attitude toward the UN’s role in peacemaking. In the years ahead, the organisation’s biggest failure may not be to fall short of lofty expectations in crisis diplomacy, but to eschew engagement altogether. 170 Richard Gowan and Daniel Forti, “ Make the U.N. great again: The uphill struggle facing the next Secretary General ”, Time , 22 August 2026. IV. Conclusion The UN’s fortunes over the next twelve months will depend in no small part on who its members select as the next Secretary-General. She or he will face considerable pressure to hit the ground running and deliver quick wins for an organisation whose credibility has waned. Doing so will require the expenditure of limited political capital on a range of priorities. Member states will no doubt push the next UN chief to translate their vision for the organisation into plans for its peace and security, development and human rights pillars. The new Secretary-General will also be tasked with stabilising the organisation’s wobbling finances and spearheading a reform agenda. If the past year at the UN was defined by transition, then the coming year may be shaped by how quickly its new leader can deliver. But the next Secretary-General cannot mend all that is fraying at the UN without renewed support from its members. At a moment of worsening geopolitical competition, a more pragmatic approach may be for states to come to a more limited interpretation of the UN’s role in world affairs. Central to that vision would be the organisation’s potential as platform to reduce global risks through communication and deconfliction, rebuilding its credibility as a peacemaker, and helping alleviate the worst of civilian suffering. The organisation will surely also have a role to play in helping the most vulnerable weather global economic shocks, including those linked both to conflict (as in the case of a prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz) and to other drivers (such as the El Niño climate pattern). Much of the debate about the UN’s work over the past year has centred on its shortcomings. That focus is understandable considering the worrying state of the international order. But as this briefing has shown, there are many crises where the UN is the only multilateral body with the mandate, legitimacy and capacity to open space for diplomacy. The organisation’s next leader would be wise to double down on those virtues. It may be an imperfect construction of the UN’s role in world affairs, but it is nonetheless an essential one. Click to expand Image Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz, UAE's President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan during a work lunch as part of the G7 summit, in Evian, eastern France, on June 16, 2026. © Ammar Abd Rabbo-Pool/SIPA/2606161433 (Sipa via AP Images) (Berlin, September 8, 2026) – German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, and other senior officials should publicly call out the United Arab Emirates’ human rights record and its role in regional conflicts when they meet President Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan in Berlin on September 10, 2026, Human Rights Watch said today. “The German government’s lack of will to publicly address the UAE’s devastating role in Sudan is deeply troubling,” said Philipp Frisch, Germany director at Human Rights Watch. “Germany led the way for robust UN investigations into atrocities in Sudan, and hosted a major conference in Berlin on the issue earlier this year. This makes its failure to address the UAE’s harmful role in Sudan all the more jarring, effectively providing a free pass for future abuses.” The UN Fact-Finding Mission on Sudan, which Germany helped establish in 2023, published a report on September 1, 2026, documenting the UAE’s support to the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), one of the warring parties in the conflict for control of Sudan since April 2023. The report concluded that the RSF was responsible for war crimes, crimes against humanity, and abuses the UN investigators found to bear “hallmarks of genocide.” UN investigators concluded that “individuals and entities operating from, registered in, or linked to the United Arab Emirates played a significant role in networks involved in the recruitment, financing, transportation and deployment of foreign military contractors and the provision of military-related support benefiting the Rapid Support Forces.” The UAE has denied these allegations. In a May 2026 report, Human Rights Watch concluded that the Abu Dhabi-based security company, Global Security Services Group had since 2024 hired hundreds of Colombian private military contractors deployed to Sudan to fight alongside the Rapid Support Forces. Private military contractors were in El Fasher, North Darfur’s capital, in October 2025, when the RSF took over the city and committed widespread atrocities. Human Rights Watch has urged Germany and other EU member states to investigate the role of the Global Security Services Group and its CEO, Mohamed Hamdan al-Zaabi, with a view to adopting targeted sanctions against them. Human Rights Watch has also urged the EU countries to adopt an EU-wide arms embargo against the UAE and publicly denounce its assistance to the Rapid Support Forces. Human Rights Watch has long documented extensive repression by the UAE at home against dissent, widespread restrictions on free expression and association, and serious abuses against migrant workers, including during the regional conflict with Iran. Emirati authorities have targeted dissidents, activists, and critics through prosecutions and lengthy prison sentences. In 2025, UAE courts confirmed the unfair conviction of 83 human rights defenders and dissidents in the country's second-largest mass trial. Among those convicted, the prominent human rights defender Ahmed Mansoor has been detained since 2017 and sentenced to lengthy prison terms in retribution for his human rights work. News organizations have reported that Germany and the UAE are expected to announce a major investment partnership during the upcoming visit. The visit will also include meetings with German arms manufactures and a state banquet. Germany's efforts to strengthen economic and security relations with the UAE should not come at the expense of addressing serious human rights concerns within the country and its role in abuses in armed conflicts, Human Rights Watch said. “How can German leaders keep a straight face when they roll out the red carpet for bin Zayed and boost security cooperation with the UAE, while the Emirates fuels atrocities in Sudan,” Frisch said. “Germany should make it clear that it stands ready to sanction UAE entities transferring arms and fighters to assist repression in Sudan, and should call for the release of Ahmed Mansoor and other unjustly jailed critics.”

Cluster Munitions: Ban Treaty Under Pressure. Click to expand Image Red sandbags cover unexploded submunitions awaiting destruction near a school in Xiang Khouang Province, Laos. © 2008 Mark Hiznay/Human Rights Watch Cluster munitions killed or injured at least 1,063 people globally in 2025. This figure is among the highest annual totals recorded by the Cluster Munition Coalition in its annual Cluster Munition Monitor. Cluster munitions typically disperse multiple explosive submunitions over a wide area. Many fail to explode on initial impact, leaving unexploded duds that can indiscriminately injure and kill like landmines for years, until they are found and destroyed.The 124 countries that are members of the Convention on Cluster Munitions at its review conference on September 14-18, 2026, should condemn the production, sale, transfer, and use of cluster munitions by other countries. (Washington, DC, September 8, 2026) – An increase in civilian deaths and injuries caused by cluster munitions should trigger united action among the 124 countries that are members of the Convention on Cluster Munitions, Human Rights Watch said today on the release of the “Cluster Munition Monitor 2026” by the Cluster Munition Coalition. Human Rights Watch is a founding member of the coalition and contributed to the report. The 150-page report assesses all countries’ adherence to the 2008 convention. Cluster munitions killed or injured at least 1,063 people globally in 2025. This figure is among the highest annual totals recorded by the Cluster Munition Coalition. The actual number is most likely higher as many casualties go unreported. New casualties were recorded in nine countries in 2025: Afghanistan, Cambodia, Iraq, Laos, Lebanon, Myanmar, Russia, Syria, and Ukraine. Cluster munitions continued to disproportionately affect civilians, whether from direct attacks or the remnants they leave behind. Civilians accounted for 87 percent of casualties recorded for 2025, where the civilian status was recorded. “It’s critically important for countries to renew their commitment to the international treaty that seeks to rid the world of the scourge of cluster munitions,” said Verity Coyle, deputy crisis, conflict and arms director at Human Rights Watch. “The clearest way to do that is for all convention member states to condemn continued production, stockpiling, and transfer of cluster munitions.” In recent months, both the United States and Türkiye have disclosed plans to transfer cluster munitions to Ukraine. Both Russia and Ukraine have used cluster munitions during the war in Ukraine. Lithuania’s withdrawal from the treaty, the first member state to do so, became final in March 2025. The country delegations meeting at the convention’s Third five-year Review Conference in Vientiane, Laos on September 14-18, 2026, should condemn the production, transfer, and use of cluster munitions by other countries and reaffirm their commitment to pressing for universal support for the ban treaty. Laos hosted the first meeting of states parties to the treaty in 2011. There has been no confirmed use of cluster munitions by any state party since the convention was adopted in May 2008. Cluster munitions were used by non-state parties Iran, Myanmar, Russia, Thailand, and Ukraine during the reporting period of mid-2025 to mid-2026. Iran repeatedly used cluster munitions in Israel in 2026, while Thailand used them in Cambodia in 2025 in the context of their border conflict. Cluster munitions were used in northern Mali in May 2026, but it was not possible to confirm who used the weapons. Cluster munitions can be fired from the ground by artillery, rockets, missiles, or mortars, or they can be dropped by aircraft. They typically open in the air, dispersing multiple explosive submunitions or bomblets over a wide area. Due to their wide area effect, the weapon cannot distinguish between civilians and combatants, especially when they are used in populated areas. In addition, many submunitions fail to explode on initial impact, leaving unexploded duds that can indiscriminately injure and kill—like landmines—for years, until they are found and destroyed. Play Video The Convention on Cluster Munitions prohibits the use, production, transfer, and stockpiling of cluster munitions and requires the clearance of explosive remnants. The Third Review Conference will address the potential for expanding treaty membership, closing funding gaps for explosive ordnance clearance programs, and providing assistance to affected communities. The Convention on Cluster Munitions has 112 states parties and 12 signatories. The most recent country to accede to the treaty was Vanuatu in September 2025. Prior to that, South Sudan and Nigeria were the last countries to become parties, joining in 2023. During the current reporting period there was evidence of cluster munition production in China, India, Israel, Myanmar, North Korea, Poland, Romania, Russia, and South Korea. Eighteen countries outside of the treaty actively produce cluster munitions, maintain the capacity to do so, or have not formally committed to never producing them. Approximately US$116 million in international and national funding was provided in 2025 to address the impact of cluster munition contamination in states parties to the convention. The US foreign assistance freeze in February 2025 disrupted the clearance of cluster munition remnants in several regions, notably in Southeast Asia. Subsequent grant terminations reduced clearance capacity in Afghanistan, Iraq, and South Sudan. Other major donors have also begun to reduce allocations and narrowed their geographic focus in response to changing political priorities. “In the face of the continued use of cluster munitions and rising civilian casualties, member countries to the convention need to send a clear message that they will stand firm in their commitment to end all use of these indiscriminate weapons,” Coyle said. The Cluster Munition Monitor 2026 is the 17th annual monitoring report by the Cluster Munition Coalition, the global coalition of nongovernmental organizations co-founded by Human Rights Watch in 2003. The report will be presented to countries attending the Third Review Conference of the Convention on Cluster Munitions in Vientiane, Laos on September 14-18.

Hungary Extends Abusive Migration State of Emergency. Click to expand Image Prime Minister of Hungary, Péter Magyar, giving a speech in the Hungarian Parliament in Budapest, August 27, 2026. © 2026 Balint Szentgallay/NurPhoto via AP Photo Hungary’s government has extended until December 31 the “state of crisis caused by mass migration,” prolonging an emergency regime introduced in 2016 despite the absence of the conditions that could justify its continued use. Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on September 4 that the government would extend the measure, which was due to expire on September 7. Magyar said the four-month extension would allow the government time to negotiate with European Union institutions on new legislation that would maintain strict border controls while complying with EU law. The state of crisis enables exceptional measures—including summary removals of asylum seekers and migrants across the border fence without an individual procedure—that violate EU and human rights law. The government’s plan to extend the state of crisis is linked to Hungary’s longstanding failure to comply with EU asylum law. In 2024, the Court of Justice of the European Union ordered Hungary to pay €200 million and an additional €1 million for every day it failed to comply with a 2020 judgment concerning access to international protection and unlawful removals. Since the formation of the new Hungarian government in May, Brussels and Budapest have discussed whether allowing temporary migration measures to lapse as well as repealing the 2016 legislation could help bring Hungary into compliance and end the accumulating financial penalties.
